<!-- file: README.md -->

# Active maintenance: a guide

In 2021, Limor Peer, Lilla Orr, and I proposed that researchers "actively maintain" their replication archives, updating the code as the software around it changes, so that published results stay reproducible for years rather than months (Peer, Orr, and Coppock 2021, *PS: Political Science & Politics*). For a long time, none of us did it, because it was a lot of work. With AI coding agents the work became cheap enough that I went back and did it for my published books and articles. This repository records how we did it, in enough detail that you could do the same for your own papers.

To have a coding agent follow the guide, paste this into it, with the bracketed parts filled in:

```text
Read https://active-maintenance-aec.github.io/guide/llms-full.txt, which is the whole guide in one file. Then follow its session-start instructions (agent/session_start.md) to help me actively maintain the replication archive for [citation], whose deposit is at [deposit DOI], in the repository at [path].
```

The guide is written for people. Each stage also has a companion file in `agent/` that says the same thing as instructions a coding agent can follow. If the two ever disagree, the version written for people is the one we meant.

## What a finished repository does

Each paper ended up with its own public repository that:

1. fetches the original deposit from its archive and checks every file against a checksum manifest (the data stay where they were deposited, and are never copied into the repository);
2. records which of the deposited scripts still run;
3. holds a maintained rewrite that reproduces every table, figure, and number in the text from the deposited data, on current software;
4. holds a *ground truth*, one generated table that compares each printed number with what the original code produces and with what the rewrite produces;
5. checks every claim in the text a second, independent way, by quoting the sentence and recomputing its number; and
6. publishes an itemized errata note, whose corrected values the code computes rather than someone typing them in.

Each repository then got a permanent DOI from Zenodo, a link back from the original deposit, and a scheduled job that reruns the whole pipeline every eight weeks, so that we hear about it when a package update moves a number.

## The stages

| Stage | What happens | What it produces |
|---|---|---|
| [0. Setup and style](stages/00_setup.md) | Gather the paper and anything else that can settle a question about it; set up the repository; write down how you like your code written. | `STYLE.md`, the published PDFs, the repository skeleton |
| [1. Archive check](stages/01_archive_check.md) | Fetch and verify the deposit, and run it as it was shipped. | `original_manifest.csv`, `download_original.R`, `archive_run_status.csv`, `archive_overwrites.csv` |
| [2. Ground truth](stages/02_ground_truth.md) | List every number the paper prints, and compare each with the archive and the rewrite. | `<paper_id>_ground_truth.csv`, `float_coverage.csv` |
| [3. Maintained rewrite](stages/03_rewrite.md) | Rewrite the code, one script per table or figure, on current packages. | `maintained/`, `maintained/output/` |
| [4. Claims](stages/04_claims.md) | Extract every claim in the text, numeric or not, and check each one a second way. | `published_claims.csv`, `in_text_claims.R` |
| [5. Errata](stages/05_errata.md) | Write up each error with a computed correction, and decide which, if any, belong in a journal notice. | `errata.qmd`, `<paper_id>_errata.pdf`, `errata_entries.csv` |
| [6. Report and publish](stages/06_publish.md) | Render the README, publish and archive the repository, link the deposit to it, and schedule the check. | `README.qmd`, a DOI, a scheduled check |

The archive check and the ground truth come before the rewrite because the rewrite is judged against them. The ground truth also starts from the article rather than from the code, for a reason Stage 2 explains: a number the pipeline never computes would otherwise never be compared with anything.

## What it cost

Our papers ranged from two-page research notes to a book, and the cost varied with them:

- **Agent time.** Most of the work is done by the agent. A typical paper took a handful of working sessions spread over a few days; a long paper with a large appendix took several times that.
- **My time.** For most papers, about 15 minutes to read the errata and decide what to do about them. For the hardest few, about two hours each, mostly spent weighing how serious an error was and digging up old files that could explain it.
- **Compute.** Most pipelines run in a few minutes. Our slowest, a large simulation study, takes most of a day on a laptop.

The early papers took far longer than the later ones, because we were working out the procedure as we went. With the procedure written down, a new paper should go faster.

## What it found

Errors turned out to be common. A small share of all the claims our papers print were wrong, but most of the papers printed at least one wrong number, and nearly all of them had a mistake of some kind once typos and reference errors are counted. Most errors were small: a number in the text left over from an earlier draft, a value rounded the wrong way, two panels of a figure in the wrong order. Errors that change a conclusion were rare, and when we found one we sent a corrigendum to the journal. If your experience is like ours, you will find errors too.

## Languages other than R

Our papers were written in R, so the templates and examples are in R. The stages, the table formats, the checks, and the rules for judging errors are not tied to R, and [`languages.md`](languages.md) lists the Stata and Python counterparts of the R tools we used. Stage 4 describes how each claim gets its verdict; the R package `excheckr` implements those rules, and nothing stops anyone from implementing them in another language.

## What is in this repository

- `stages/`: one file per stage, with its purpose, inputs, outputs, checks, and the judgment calls it involves.
- `schemas/`: the columns and allowed values of every table the procedure produces.
- `rules/`: the judgments that kept coming up (what counts as an erratum, rounding, simulation noise, and when an error needs a journal notice).
- `templates/`: starting files for a new repository.
- `agent/`: the stages as instructions for a coding agent.
- `traps.md`: problems we ran into more than once, and how we got around them.
- `languages.md`: Stata and Python counterparts of the R tools.
- `examples/`: finished repositories from our collection, and an example `STYLE.md`.

## License

CC0. Take whatever is useful.


<!-- file: stages/00_setup.md -->

# Stage 0: Setup and style

Before writing any code, we gathered everything that might help answer a question about the paper, set up the repository, and wrote down how we wanted the new code to look.

## The published record

We worked from the publisher's rendered PDFs: the article itself (the version of record), the online appendix, and any corrigendum already published. A published corrigendum is an analysis too, and we checked it against its own materials like everything else.

We learned to avoid preprints and accepted manuscripts as sources for published values. They often differ from the final article in small ways (a number updated in proofs, a table reordered, a sentence reworded), and comparing against the wrong version produced errata that weren't real.

## The deposit

Next we found the replication deposit (ours were on Dataverse and OSF) and recorded its DOI. We left the data where they were. Stage 1 writes a script that downloads the deposit and checks each file against a manifest, so the journal's archive stays the single source for the data.

## Materials outside the deposit

Some of the most useful evidence was not in the deposit at all. Depending on the paper, we had:

- the final production files sent to the publisher (`.tex` or `.docx`);
- the proofs, with our marked-up corrections;
- the accepted manuscript;
- older scripts and intermediate files from our working folders.

None of these fed into the rewrite. What they did was settle questions the deposit couldn't. When the text printed a wrong number, was it a typo, or a number left over from an earlier run? Did an error enter during typesetting, or was it already in our manuscript? What did the code look like when we wrote the paper? When one of these files settled a question, the erratum records it as its source (`authors_archive` or `proof`; see [the errata schema](../schemas/errata_entries.md)).

Two lessons from using them. A `.tex` file from a working folder can be a draft from before copyediting; we treated one as the published text only when its compiled PDF matched the publisher's byte for byte. And because files that were never public can't be checked by a reader, we used them to explain errors, and kept each correction itself grounded in the published article and the deposited data.

## The repository

Each repository has:

- a single entry point (`run_all.R` for us; a master `.do` file or a Python script would do the same job) that runs everything in order and stops at the first failure;
- paths relative to the repository root (we used the `here` package), so the code runs on anyone's machine;
- a `.gitignore` that keeps the downloaded deposit out of version control;
- a license. We used CC0 for the code and did not redistribute the data.

Our folder layout:

```
run_all.R
download_original.R
original_manifest.csv
STYLE.md
maintained/            # the rewrite, one script per table or figure
maintained/output/     # everything the rewrite writes
ground_truth/          # the comparison tables and the scripts that build them
errata.qmd
README.qmd
```

## Style investigation

A rewrite is code that you and others will be reading for years, so it should look like code you'd write today. My own habits have changed a lot since graduate school, and the rewrite was a chance to bring old projects up to how I work now. An agent can't know what that means without reading some of your code, so we made the question an explicit step.

1. **Gather some recent code** that you're happy with, ideally from more than one project.
2. **Have the agent draft a `STYLE.md`** from what it reads. Ours covered, with examples drawn from the code itself:
   - how scripts are organized (one per table or figure, cleaning separate from analysis, a shared helpers file, a short header comment);
   - naming of files, objects, and columns;
   - how data get reshaped, joined, and recoded;
   - modeling defaults (estimators, standard errors, packages);
   - figures (theme, how intervals are drawn, file formats, and a CSV of the plotted values saved next to each figure);
   - tables;
   - anything to avoid.
3. **Read the draft, fix it, and approve it.** The draft gets some things wrong, and fixing those turned out to be where most of the value was. The approved file is committed, and the rewrite follows it.

`STYLE.md` covers how the code *looks*. A few things about what the rewrite *does* stay the same whatever your style:

- it reproduces every number, table, and figure the paper prints, or documents why it can't;
- it runs on current versions of every package;
- it reads the data exactly as deposited;
- it keeps the paper's original estimator, specification, sample, and seed, even where you'd now choose differently (a choice you would make differently today isn't an error; see [what counts as an erratum](../rules/erratum.md));
- it never uses a published number as an input.

When a style preference and one of these conflict, the paper's choices win. The case we hit most often: my current default standard errors differ from what some of the older papers used, and the rewrites kept the originals.

There's an example `STYLE.md` from our collection in [`examples/STYLE_example.md`](../examples/STYLE_example.md). It is one person's taste, and is there to show the level of detail that worked for us.

## Done when

The repository exists with its entry point and layout, the published PDFs are in hand, the deposit DOI is recorded, and an approved `STYLE.md` is committed.


<!-- file: stages/01_archive_check.md -->

# Stage 1: Archive check

In this stage we pinned down exactly what each deposit contains and found out whether its code still runs, before starting the rewrite.

It helped to keep two questions apart. *Does the archive run?* is answered here, by executing it. *Does the archive reproduce the paper?* is answered in Stage 2, by comparing what it produces with what the paper prints. The two come apart more often than you might expect: some of our archives ran cleanly and reproduced little, and others failed on the first line yet reproduced everything once that line was fixed.

## The manifest and the download script

For each deposit we wrote `original_manifest.csv`, one row per file, from the archive's own API rather than by hand. For Dataverse:

`file, directory_label, dataverse_file_id, file_persistent_id, bytes, md5_served, md5_published, unf, served_as`

For OSF:

`file, directory_label, osf_file_id, bytes, md5_served, md5_published, sha256_published`

`md5_served` is the checksum of the bytes the archive actually sends, and `md5_published` is the checksum in the archive's metadata. They usually agree. They don't when Dataverse has converted a tabular upload to its own format and serves the converted version by default; in that case we recorded both and asked for the original format.

Then `download_original.R`:

1. downloads every file in the manifest into `original/`, which git ignores;
2. stops if any file's size or served checksum differs from the manifest;
3. prints, without stopping, any disagreement with the published checksum;
4. stops if `original/` contains a file the manifest doesn't list, hidden files included;
5. unpacks any zip or RAR file into its own regenerated folder and checks the contents against a second manifest.

`run_all.R` runs this script first. It's the one check in the whole pipeline that comes with a deadline. If a deposit ever stops verifying, the archive has changed the files, released a new version, or withdrawn the deposit, and the sooner you find out which, the better. At that point the manifest may be the only public record of what the deposit held.

## Running the archive as shipped

We ran each deposited script in a scratch copy of the deposit (never in the downloaded folder itself) and recorded what happened in `ground_truth/archive_run_status.csv`:

`pass, script, role, exit_status, outcome, stopped_at`

- `pass` is `as_shipped` (the deposit exactly as downloaded) or `stripped` (only the raw data and the code, with any intermediate files the deposit included removed). We ran both, because a deposit that includes its own intermediate files can make a script look fine when the script that should have produced those files is broken.
- `role` is `cleaning`, `analysis`, or `other`. A helper file that is only ever sourced by other scripts gets no row, since it never runs on its own.
- `outcome` is `clean`, `error`, `timeout`, or `not_run`. Scripts we couldn't run at all (several needed Stata, which we didn't have) still got rows, with `not_run` and the reason in `stopped_at`.

Where it mattered, we ran under the conditions of the paper's day. R changed its default random-number sampler in version 3.6.0 (April 2019), so for older code we set `RNGkind(sample.kind = "Rounding")` when checking whether the archive reproduced its own published draws. The rewrite uses the current default, and any number that moves because of it is recorded as an `environment` difference (see [Stage 2](02_ground_truth.md)).

## What the run writes

Before running, we searched the deposited code for anything that writes a file, joining lines first, since a write call split across two lines is easy to miss. After running, we compared every file's modification time and checksum with the manifest and recorded what had changed in `ground_truth/archive_overwrites.csv`:

`pass, file, effect, matches_deposit`

`effect` is `added`, `overwritten`, `rebuilt`, `withheld` (an intermediate removed for the stripped pass that nothing rebuilt), or `deleted`, and `matches_deposit` says whether a file the run rewrote came out identical to the deposited one. When a run overwrote a deposited output with something different, that told us something: either the deposited output came from different code than what was deposited, or the software had moved. Running in a scratch copy is what made this table possible, and it also kept the runs from quietly altering the deposit we were trying to document.

## Diagnosing failures

When a script failed, we recorded why, and left the deposit as it was: the deposit is the published record, and its failures are part of what we were documenting. The causes we saw most often, roughly in order: a function removed or renamed in a package update; a package that no longer installs; an absolute path from the author's computer; a file the authors never deposited; and a script that depends on an intermediate file no deposited script creates. We learned to treat a "deprecated function" warning as a hypothesis about the cause; several times it turned out not to be the real problem.

## Done when

The manifest verifies, the download script stops on any mismatch, and every deposited script has a row in `archive_run_status.csv` for each pass.


<!-- file: stages/02_ground_truth.md -->

# Stage 2: Ground truth

The ground truth is one table, built by a script, that lists every number the paper prints and compares each with the value the original code produces and the value the maintained rewrite produces. Every erratum about a number traces back to a row in it, and every claim that the rewrite reproduces the paper rests on it.

We settled on two principles for it, both learned the hard way.

**Start from the article.** We list what the paper prints first, and only then join that list to what the pipeline computes. Our earliest attempts went the other way, starting from the code's output, and they were blind to any number the code never computed. Those turned out to be some of the most error-prone numbers of all: values typed into the text by hand, or left over from an earlier draft.

**Generate it rather than type it.** The only values in the table that a person types are the printed ones, transcribed from the published page. The archive's values come from running the deposited code, the rewrite's values are read from its output files, and the verdicts are computed. In one early repository, the comparison values had been typed in by hand too, and every row "matched", which meant the table couldn't have detected a problem if there had been one.

## The table

`ground_truth/<paper_id>_ground_truth.csv` is written by `ground_truth/build_ground_truth.R`, which `run_all.R` runs last:

`paper_id, claim_id, location, claim_type, claim, value_paper, digits, value_script, match, value_rewrite, match_rewrite, holds, defect_locus, disposition, disposition_reason, notes`

- `location` says where the number is printed: a table or figure, a page and paragraph, a footnote, or an appendix section.
- `value_paper` is the number exactly as printed, stored as text. Reading it as a number throws information away: `0.80` becomes `0.8`, `-0.00` becomes `0`, and the printed precision, which is part of what the paper claims, is lost. We had this happen in several repositories before we started forcing the column to be read as text everywhere.
- `digits` is the precision the page prints, recorded for each row.
- `value_script` comes from running the deposited code in Stage 1, and is left empty where the archive couldn't be run.
- `value_rewrite` is read from the rewrite's output at full precision.
- `match`, `match_rewrite`, and `holds` take the values `TRUE`, `FALSE`, or empty.

The full definitions are in [`schemas/ground_truth.md`](../schemas/ground_truth.md).

## When two numbers match

A computed value matches a printed one when, rounded to the precision the page prints, it gives the same digits. Before comparing, both sides get the same clean-up: a missing leading zero restored, a typographic minus sign replaced, thousands separators removed, and a negative zero treated as zero. A tiny tolerance (`1e-9`) absorbs floating-point representation, and nothing else.

Three refinements came up often enough to write down:

- **Hedged numbers.** When the text itself hedges ("about 40 percent", "roughly", "nearly", "on the order of"), we compared within half a step of the sentence's own precision. When the text states an approximate number without a hedge, we held it to its printed digits: a sentence that says 40 percent about a value of 38 percent is an error.
- **Differences of printed values.** When the text reports a difference between two printed cells, we allowed one unit in the last digit, since each cell was rounded separately.
- **The archive's precision.** We compared the archive's value at the coarser of the page's precision and the precision at which the deposited code itself prints.

More detail and examples are in [`rules/rounding.md`](../rules/rounding.md).

## Numbers that come from random draws

Bootstrap intervals, randomization-inference p-values, simulated power, and anything else based on random draws can differ from run to run, and between software versions even with the same seed. Before putting a difference down to randomness, we checked that the procedure actually draws at random; more than once, a difference that looked like noise was a deterministic bug. For a value the paper reports without a seed, we compared it with the distribution of that value over many seeds, left `match_rewrite` empty, and recorded in `holds` whether the printed value was consistent with that distribution. A printed value far outside any reasonable draw counts as an error; one inside the range doesn't. See [`rules/stochastic.md`](../rules/stochastic.md).

## Where the problem is: `defect_locus`

Each row where a comparison fails (`match`, `match_rewrite`, or `holds` is `FALSE`) records where the problem lies:

| `defect_locus` | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `paper_internal` | The printed text is wrong: the code produces one number and the page prints another (a typo, a stale number, a rounding slip, a transposed cell). |
| `archive` | The deposited code is wrong: it produces a number that a corrected computation doesn't, and the page printed what the code produced. |
| `environment` | The software changed: the deposited code, run today, gives a different number than it did then. |
| `rewrite` | The maintained rewrite is wrong. We fixed these, so none should remain at the end. |
| `upstream` | The problem is in something the paper relied on, such as a dataset or an estimate it reused. |
| `unresolved` | We looked, and couldn't tell. |

The rule cuts both ways: a failing row gets a locus, and a row where everything matches doesn't. A row with no verdict, such as an unseeded value, may or may not.

One case is easy to miss. Sometimes the page, the archive, and the rewrite all agree, yet the number is wrong, because the deposited code has a bug and the rewrite faithfully reproduced it before the bug was found. Every comparison "matches", and the paper is still in error. We record those rows with the locus `archive`, and only when an erratum names them.

We set the locus where each row is built, rather than as a default for the whole table, and put any second contributing cause in `notes`.

## What was done about it: `disposition`

Each row with a defect also records what happened to it:

| `disposition` | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `corrected_here` | An entry in this repository's errata corrects it. This one is computed from the errata, never entered by hand. |
| `corrected_by_journal` | A published corrigendum or erratum corrects it. |
| `documented_only` | Recorded here and deliberately not corrected (a value within simulation noise, for example). |
| `not_corrected` | Known, and left uncorrected for a stated reason. |
| empty | Nobody has decided yet. |

The three judgment values come with a `disposition_reason`. The build stops if any `paper_internal` row has no disposition, since an error in the printed text that nobody has decided about is unfinished business.

The dispositions line up with the choice an author faces for each error: fix it in your own errata, send it to the journal, or record it and move on. [`rules/severity.md`](../rules/severity.md) describes how we made that choice.

## Coverage

Our first coverage check asked only whether every table had at least one row in the ground truth, and it passed while missing most of the numbers on some tables. We now report coverage table by table and figure by figure, as a fraction, in `ground_truth/float_coverage.csv`:

`float, published_numbers, covered, reproduced_by_rewrite, reproduced_by_archive, plotted, plotted_reproduced, note`

- The list of tables and figures comes from the article itself, and we checked it in both directions: every table and figure in the article has a row, and every row names one that the article contains.
- `published_numbers` counts the numbers printed on each table or figure, and `covered` counts how many of them have a row in the ground truth.
- For a figure that prints no numbers, what it plots is the claim, so we counted the plotted quantities and how many the rewrite reproduces. A figure never got a pass just for having no printed numbers.
- The README reports each covered fraction.

Two things caught us out when joining the article's list to the pipeline's output. A join that silently matches nothing produces empty values that look like "couldn't check" rather than "missing", and a join that matches one row to several quietly duplicates rows. We checked every join in both directions and confirmed that each matched one row to one row. We also stopped selecting rows by their published value, which guarantees a match.

Finally, we read multi-column tables from the rendered page rather than from text extracted from the PDF. Text extraction can scramble columns, and a misread cell produces an erratum that isn't real.

## Done when

The build script runs as the last step of `run_all.R`, and it stops if any printed value has been read as a number, if any failing row lacks a `defect_locus` or any matching row has one, if any `paper_internal` row lacks a disposition, if any join is not one-to-one, or if any published table or figure is missing from `float_coverage.csv`.


<!-- file: stages/03_rewrite.md -->

# Stage 3: Maintained rewrite

The rewrite is new code that reproduces every table, figure, and number in the paper from the deposited data, on current software, written the way `STYLE.md` describes. It is the part of the project that keeps the paper usable: when a package changes next year, this is the code that gets updated.

## Shape

We wrote one script per table or figure, named for what it produces, with cleaning kept separate from analysis and shared functions in a single `maintained/helpers.R`. Every script writes to `maintained/output/`. Next to each figure we also save a CSV of every quantity it plots, because a figure file can't be compared with anything, while a CSV of its points can. Tables are written both formatted and unrounded, so that later stages compare full-precision values rather than what a table package chose to print.

## Three rules we held to

**No published number goes in.** The rewrite computes everything from the deposited data. When a script seemed to need a number from the paper (a threshold, a sample size, a cut point), that was nearly always a sign that the computation upstream of it was missing. The one exception is a number that is itself a claim about the data, such as "fewer than 5 percent of respondents failed the attention check", which a dedicated script checks rather than uses.

**No script skips its own work.** A script that checks whether its output already exists and returns early can pass every test while being broken. Ours always recompute.

**Every "can't be computed" is a claim to test.** Several times a comment in the archive, or in an early draft of our own rewrite, said that some number couldn't be reproduced from the deposit, and it turned out it could. We treated such comments as hypotheses, and checked them.

## Errors versus choices

The rewrite corrects unambiguous coding errors: a typo in a variable name, a wrong index, the wrong column, a covariate left out of a specification the paper describes. It does not revisit analysis decisions. If the paper used a particular estimator, specification, sample, or set of standard errors, the rewrite uses the same one, even where we would now choose differently. A choice we'd make differently today isn't an error, and treating it as one would turn the errata into a second paper.

The line isn't always sharp. One case that came up repeatedly: a regression silently dropped collinear covariates, so the model actually estimated differed from the one the paper describes. We counted that as an error, because the paper's own description says what was intended. When we couldn't tell which of two deposited values the authors meant, we wrote the finding up as a note for the authors to decide, rather than picking one.

Each correction the rewrite makes shows up in the ground truth as a row where the rewrite disagrees with the archive (`match_rewrite = FALSE`, locus `archive`), and in the errata in Stage 5. We were careful not to carry a typo forward into the new code just because the old code had it; the point is that the rewrite is right.

## Software changes

The rewrite uses current packages and the current random-number generator. When either moves a published number, the ground truth records it with the locus `environment`. A few of these surprised us. A function can keep its name and arguments while changing what it computes: one test function, given a regression fit from a newer package, quietly began using a different variance estimator, with no warning. Converting an old grid-building function to its modern equivalent transposed a grid, which showed up only when we laid the new figure beside the published one. We now compare every rendered figure with the published version by eye, in addition to comparing the numbers.

## The same answer twice

We ran `run_all.R` twice from fresh sessions, checked that both runs exited cleanly, and confirmed that the second run left the output folder byte-for-byte unchanged. PDFs embed a creation timestamp, so we blank it when writing figures; otherwise every run "changes" every figure. A pipeline that gives a different answer on the second run has an unseeded random draw or depends on something outside the repository, and both need fixing before the comparisons mean anything.

## Done when

`run_all.R` runs from a clean session, every table and figure in the paper has a script that produces it, no published value is an input, and two runs in a row leave `maintained/output/` unchanged.


<!-- file: stages/04_claims.md -->

# Stage 4: Claims

The ground truth checks numbers against the pipeline. Stage 4 checks the *text*: every claim the article makes, numeric or not, gets extracted, classified, and checked a second way, by code that quotes the sentence and recomputes what it says.

We added this stage after finding that the ground truth alone missed a large share of the errors. Rerunning the code found well under half of the errata in our collection; reading the articles against themselves, their appendices, and their code found about as many again. A pipeline that reproduces every table can still sit under a paper whose text says something the tables don't.

## Extracting the claims

`ground_truth/published_claims.csv` lists every claim in the article and appendix:

`claim_id, location, claim_type, claim, value_paper, digits, comparison, expect, needs_block, notes`

We built it in two passes. The first extracts every numeric token from the text mechanically, and a second sweep catches numbers written as words ("two-thirds of respondents", "in all but one study"). Each candidate is then classified by hand:

| `claim_type` | What it is |
|---|---|
| `pipeline` | A number the analysis produces: an estimate, a standard error, a p-value, a sample size. |
| `descriptive` | A claim about the results that may print no number at all (see below). |
| `definitional` | A number that defines the design: the number of treatment arms, a scale's range, a survey wave's date. |
| `structural` | A number about the paper itself: "three experiments", "Table 2 shows". |
| `transcribed` | A number quoted from somewhere else, such as another study's estimate. |

`needs_block` is `TRUE` for every `pipeline` and `descriptive` claim, and for the `definitional` and `structural` claims the pipeline can actually reach. `value_paper` is stored as text, for the reasons given in [Stage 2](02_ground_truth.md).

## Claims without numbers

The claims most likely to change a reader's conclusion often print no number. A numeric sweep can't see them, so we read for them directly, looking for the verbs and phrases of comparison and inference:

- **significance**: "statistically significant", "cannot be distinguished from zero";
- **direction**: "larger among Republicans", "the effect reverses";
- **order**: "the largest effect", "smaller than the misinformation effect";
- **persistence**: "remains detectable after two weeks";
- **counts in words**: "most of the 24 experiments", "in every study".

Each becomes a `descriptive` claim, and its check tests the statement against the rewrite's output: is the interval clear of zero, is one estimate larger than the other, does the effect still appear at the later wave. The first error we found that changed a conclusion was a claim of this kind. An article reported that the effects of fact-checks remained detectable more than two weeks after exposure; once a coding error was corrected, the two-week estimate could not be distinguished from zero. No single number in that sentence was the problem. The claim was.

## The second check

`maintained/in_text_claims.R` has one block for each claim that needs one. Each block quotes the sentence verbatim and recomputes the claim from the rewrite's output files or its cleaned data. It never refits a model, and it never reads the ground truth, so that the two checks are independent: the ground truth compares tables with the pipeline, while this file compares the prose with the pipeline. When both agree that a number is wrong, we can be confident it is.

Each block prints one line in a fixed format:

`CLAIM <claim_id> = <computed value> || [verdict] <label>`

The verdicts that pass are:

| verdict | meaning |
|---|---|
| `match` | The computed value, at the printed precision, equals the printed value. |
| `corrected` | The printed value is wrong, and an erratum already corrects it (so the check expects the corrected value). |
| `range` | The claim states a range or a bound, and the block tests that the computed value falls within it. |
| `derived` | The printed number is computed from other printed numbers, and the block tests that the arithmetic holds. |
| `hedged` | A `descriptive` claim, such as a hedged number ("about", "roughly"), whose printed digits the computed value does not reproduce. The check does not apply the half-step bound from [`rules/rounding.md`](../rules/rounding.md) on its own, so the block must. |
| `shape` | A claim that prints no number, or a claim about direction, order, or significance that the block has tested. |
| `absent` | The claim refers to something the pipeline was never going to produce, and this is recorded. |

Only `match`, `corrected`, and the failing verdicts are decided by the check itself. The others record a test the block has to carry out, so a block that declares one without testing anything still passes; these blocks deserve the closest reading.

The verdicts that fail are `MISMATCH` (the value is wrong and no erratum covers it), `STALE` (an erratum says the value is wrong, but the pipeline now reproduces the printed one), `DRIFT` (an erratum corrects the claim, and the value now agrees with neither the printed value nor the correction), and `MISSING` (a claim that needs a block has none). The file ends with a summary line that counts each verdict, and the run fails on any failing verdict.

In R, the package `excheckr` implements these verdicts (`claim_start()`, `claim()`, and `claim_summary()`). The table above is the specification, and the logic is simple enough to rewrite in Stata or Python; see [`languages.md`](../languages.md).

## Making sure every claim is checked

An early lesson: a claims file can look complete while checking nothing. In R, a script run with `source()` prints nothing unless told to, so dozens of blocks appeared to cover their claims while producing no output at all. The check that caught it was simple, and we now run it every time: run the file on its own, count the `CLAIM` lines it prints, and confirm that the count equals the number of `needs_block` rows in `published_claims.csv`, and that the printed IDs are exactly the declared ones.

We also reconcile the two instruments with each other. Every claim that appears in both the ground truth and the claims file must have the same printed value and the same classification, and where both compute a value, they must agree. Agreement has a limit worth stating: two checks can agree on a number and still both compute the wrong quantity for the sentence. The sentence-by-sentence quotes in the claims file are there so that a person can read each block and confirm that it computes what the sentence actually says.

## Text with no counterpart in the output

Some claims refer to something the rewrite doesn't produce. We sorted these into a few cases:

- **A gap in the rewrite**: the quantity should have been written out. We added it to the relevant script.
- **The deposited code contradicts the claim**, or never computed it: the claim gets the locus `archive`.
- **Nothing in the paper or the deposit identifies the quantity**: we recorded that, and did not invent a computation to check it against.
- **The deposit was never going to contain it** (a date, a design detail): it is `definitional`, with no locus.

## Done when

Every claim in the article and appendix is in `published_claims.csv`, every claim that needs a check has one, the printed count equals the declared count, the two instruments agree, and the summary line shows no failing verdicts.


<!-- file: stages/05_errata.md -->

# Stage 5: Errata

Every error the earlier stages turn up is written up in one itemized errata note per paper, rendered to a PDF that sits at the top of the repository and, in our case, also on my website. The corrected values in it are computed by the code at the time the note is rendered, so if a package update ever moves a number, the errata move with it.

## What counts as an erratum

We counted any statement printed in the article, its appendix, or its references that is wrong, however small. That includes:

- a wrong number, or a number left over from an earlier draft;
- a value rounded the wrong way at the printed precision (the text printed 0.23 for a value of 0.2230);
- a description of a method, sample, or variable that doesn't match what was done;
- a label, a legend, or a panel order that is wrong;
- a cross-reference to the wrong table;
- spelling and typesetting mistakes;
- reference-list errors, which were common (much of my early bibliography came from search-engine citations that were themselves wrong).

We left out three things. A value that differs from our computation only within the estimator's own noise is not an error (see [`rules/stochastic.md`](../rules/stochastic.md)). A finding we couldn't judge either way is recorded as `unresolved` in the ground truth rather than corrected. An analysis choice we would now make differently is not an error at all (see [`rules/erratum.md`](../rules/erratum.md)).

When the prose disagreed with the paper's own table and our computation supported the table, we corrected the sentence to match the table.

## The note

`errata.qmd` renders `<paper_id>_errata.pdf` and writes `errata_entries.csv`, one row per entry:

`entry, class, source, form, title, location, published, corrected, note, claim_ids, corrected_values, values_in_spans`

- `class` says what kind of error it is: `quantity`, `description`, `interpretation`, `definition`, `label`, `float`, `cross_reference`, `wording`, `spelling`, `typography`, or `bibliographic`.
- `source` says how we found it: `pipeline` (the rewrite computed a different value), `reading` (reading the article against itself, its appendix, and its code), `reference_audit` (checking every reference against Crossref), `publisher_record` (an earlier published correction), `authors_archive` (our own files outside the deposit), or `proof` (the proofs or accepted manuscript).
- `form` is `full` (the published and corrected passages, quoted in full), `brief` (a one-line correction), or `note` (an explanation with no replacement text).
- `published` and `corrected` quote the passage before and after, with the changed values marked; `claim_ids` ties each entry to rows in the ground truth and the claims file.

Each entry's corrected values are computed from the rewrite's output when the note renders. The build checks that every claim an entry names exists, that only `quantity` entries carry corrected values, that every corrected value appears in the corrected text, and that no entry "corrects" a claim the pipeline reproduces. One rule caught several mistakes of ours: a corrected value must never render identically to the published one at the printed precision, because then there is nothing to correct.

Entries are numbered by severity, with the errors that matter most first, and once a note is public its numbering only grows: new entries are added at the end, so that anyone citing "entry 3" keeps pointing at the same thing.

Every quotation in the note was checked against an image of the published page. Text extracted from a PDF can drop characters, merge columns, or mangle symbols, and an erratum that misquotes the article is itself an error.

## Whether a conclusion changes

The pipeline can tell you that a number is wrong. Whether that changes a conclusion of the paper is a judgment, and we left it to the authors. When an entry did change a conclusion, the note says so plainly at the top.

## Which errors go to the journal

Most of the errors we found were embarrassing but trivial, and the scientific contribution of each paper stands without them. Sending dozens of journals a correction for every typo and rounding slip would bury the editors and devalue corrections as a signal. We used three tiers:

1. **Every error** goes in the errata note, beside the maintained code, where anyone reading the repository will find it.
2. **An error that changes the direction or implications of a finding a reader would rely on** also goes to the journal as a corrigendum, whether or not the finding appears in the abstract. In our experience, errors that meet this bar are rare.
3. **Retraction** is for findings that can no longer be relied on at all.

When a corrigendum was warranted, we used it to correct the related errors in the same article as well. The reasoning behind the tiers is in [`rules/severity.md`](../rules/severity.md), and the `disposition` column in the ground truth records which tier each error landed in.

## Done when

`errata.qmd` renders without error, every corrected value is computed rather than typed, every quotation has been checked against the published page, the build's checks pass, and every `paper_internal` row in the ground truth has a disposition.


<!-- file: stages/06_publish.md -->

# Stage 6: Report and publish

The last stage makes the work findable and keeps it working: a README that explains the repository to a stranger, a permanent DOI, a link from the original deposit, and a scheduled check that reruns everything.

## The README

`README.qmd` renders to the repository's `README.md` (and, for us, to a PDF report as well). We wrote it for someone who has never heard of the project and has just landed on the repository from the article. Ours cover, in order: what the repository is, with a table of verified DOIs (article, deposit, and this repository's own); how to run it; an overview of the paper; whether the deposited archive runs; the errata, with a pointer to the PDF; the ground truth and how much of each table and figure it covers; the two claim checks; the rewrite; and the software environment.

Every quantity in the README's prose is computed by an inline chunk rather than typed. Ours started out with typed numbers, and they went stale quickly: one README misstated a subset count by 150,000 after the pipeline changed underneath it.

We kept the README about the paper, and left out the history of the project: no "an earlier version of this repository found", no dates of earlier passes. A reader who never saw an earlier mistake doesn't need to hear about its correction.

## The repository

Each paper got its own public repository, licensed CC0, with `run_all.R` as the entry point. The deposit itself is never copied in; `download_original.R` fetches it. Before publishing, we ran the whole pipeline once more and confirmed that it left no stray or changed files, and we checked file paths against a case-sensitive file system, since one repository worked on a Mac and failed on Linux over the capitalization of a single file name.

## A permanent DOI

GitHub isn't an archive, and neither is a personal website. We archived each repository at Zenodo, which mints a *concept DOI* that always resolves to the latest version, plus a version DOI for each release. Zenodo makes a new version only when you publish a GitHub release, so routine maintenance doesn't mint new DOIs; we cut a release when the errata or the maintained code changed in a way worth archiving.

A `.zenodo.json` in the repository sets the record's title, creators, license, and related identifiers: the article (`isSupplementTo`), the original deposit (`isDerivedFrom`), and the GitHub repository itself. One thing caught us: once `.zenodo.json` lists related identifiers, Zenodo stops adding the link to the GitHub repository on its own, so it has to be listed explicitly.

The concept DOI then goes in the README and in the errata note, so that the PDF, wherever it travels, points back to the maintained code.

## Linking the deposit back

A reader who starts from the article follows its DOI to the original deposit. For them to find the maintained version, the deposit has to point to it. On Dataverse we added a line to each deposit's *Related Material* field, giving the Zenodo DOI and the repository URL. A metadata-only change publishes a minor version (1.1, say) with the files untouched. On OSF, which has no such field, the line went into the project description.

Some details from doing this for all of our deposits:

- Deposits in your own Dataverse collection can be published directly. Deposits in a journal's collection usually go to the journal's curators for review, which on Harvard Dataverse means agreeing to a short attestation and waiting.
- Some older deposits lacked fields that Dataverse now requires (a subject, a contact email), and couldn't be saved until those were filled in.
- Deposits made by a coauthor or by the journal can only be edited by them.
- Harvard Dataverse runs an automated metadata check on publication, and it held one of ours for staff review.

## The scheduled check

Active maintenance only works if someone notices when the code stops working. Each repository carries a short GitHub Actions workflow that calls a shared one in [`active-maintenance-aec/maintenance`](https://github.com/active-maintenance-aec/maintenance), which reruns `run_all.R` on current R and current packages, every eight weeks, with the repositories staggered so that a handful run each week. The check fails if the pipeline breaks or if any committed file it judges changes.

A few choices made the check useful rather than noisy:

- **Numbers are judged; figure files are not.** A PDF or PNG drawn on Linux is never byte-identical to one drawn on a Mac, so figure files are counted but don't fail the check. Every figure's plotted values are saved as a CSV, and those are judged.
- **Floating-point noise is forgiven.** Linux and macOS differ in the last bits of some floating-point results, so a CSV whose only differences fall within a relative tolerance of one in a million is counted as noise.
- **The schedule stays alive.** GitHub disables a scheduled workflow after 60 days without activity in the repository, which a maintained repository can easily go. The workflow re-enables itself every week.
- **Very slow pipelines get a shorter run.** GitHub limits a job to six hours. One of our pipelines takes far longer than that, so on GitHub it skips its slowest deposited scripts and judges everything else, and the full run happens locally.

When the check fails, the cause is usually a package update. The rewrite is meant to be current code, so the response is to update the rewrite, not to pin the old package version; if a published number moves, the ground truth records it as an `environment` difference and the errata note updates when it next renders.

## Done when

The README renders with every number computed, the repository is public, its Zenodo DOI resolves and appears in the README and the errata, the original deposit links to it, and the scheduled check has passed at least once.


<!-- file: rules/erratum.md -->

# What counts as an erratum

An erratum is a statement printed in the article, its appendix, or its references that is wrong. The [Stage 5](../stages/05_errata.md) list of what that covers is long on purpose: wrong numbers, numbers rounded the wrong way, misdescriptions, bad labels, wrong cross-references, typos, and bad references all count, however small. Most of the work of applying the rule was in the cases at its edges, which this page collects.

## Errors versus choices

The line we drew is between implementation and analysis. An erratum is a place where the paper did not do what it says it did, or says something its own analysis does not support. A choice we would make differently today is not an erratum, however strongly we now prefer the alternative.

Errors, in our usage:

- a typo in a variable name, a wrong index, or the wrong column;
- a standardization that divides by the wrong group's standard deviation;
- a covariate left in (or out of) a specification the paper describes differently, such as wave 2 outcomes copied into a wave 3 model;
- a number in the text left over from an earlier draft of the analysis;
- a sentence that describes the sample, the estimator, or a variable differently from what the code does.

Choices, which we left alone:

- the estimator, the standard errors, and the covariate set the paper used;
- the sample definition, including exclusions we would not make now;
- the outcome scaling, the plotting decisions, and the tables a paper chose to show.

The rewrite keeps every one of those choices (see [Stage 3](../stages/03_rewrite.md)). An errata note that relitigated them would become a second paper, and a reader could no longer tell the mistakes from the second thoughts.

## The gray area: collinear covariates

A regression with collinear covariates is rank-deficient, and the software drops a column to fit it. Which column it drops depends on column order and on the software version, so the printed estimate depends on an accident rather than on a decision anyone made. The paper's own description of the model says what was intended, and the fitted model is not that model. We ruled that these count as errata and corrected them.

## When everything matches and the paper is still wrong

Agreement among the page, the archive, and the rewrite shows consistency, not correctness. A paper can print exactly what its code produced while the code has a bug, and a rewrite written against the archive can inherit the same bug. One paper summed vote shares across merged precincts instead of recomputing them, and every comparison matched. Reading the deposited code, rather than only running it, found that error and others like it. Such an error is still an erratum; in the ground truth it carries the locus `archive` even though every comparison reads `TRUE`.

## The text against its own tables

When a sentence disagreed with the paper's own table and our computation supported the table, we corrected the sentence. When we could not tell which of two deposited values the authors meant (two versions of a variable, say, each defensible), we did not pick one. We wrote the finding up as a note for the authors to decide.

## Approximations

A number the text hedges ("about", "roughly", "nearly", "on the order of") is held to what the hedge could reasonably mean. A number the text states without a hedge is held to its printed digits, even when the true value is close. A sentence that says effects run "between 0.30 and 0.50 standard deviations", about estimates of 0.283 and 0.522, is an erratum: both estimates fall outside the interval as written. The details, including how wide a hedge is allowed to be, are in [`rounding.md`](rounding.md).

## What we left out

- **Differences within simulation noise.** A value from a random procedure that falls inside the distribution of that value over seeds is not an error. See [`stochastic.md`](stochastic.md).
- **Findings we could not judge.** When we looked and could not tell whether the paper was wrong, the ground truth records `defect_locus = unresolved` and the errata say nothing. An erratum we were not sure of would itself be an error.
- **Defects the reader never sees.** A bug in the deposited code that the rewrite repairs but that never reached a printed number is recorded in the ground truth (`documented_only`) and is not an erratum, because nothing on the page is wrong.

## Who decides

The agent proposes and the author decides. Whether a discrepancy is an error or a choice, and whether a correction changes a conclusion, were the author's calls in every case, and for any correction sent to a journal they were the coauthors' calls too. For most papers these decisions took about a quarter of an hour; the hardest took a couple of hours each.


<!-- file: rules/rounding.md -->

# Rounding

The rule in one sentence: a computed value matches a printed one when, formatted to the precision the page prints, it gives the same digits. Everything below is about applying that rule without fooling yourself in either direction.

## Keep the printed value as a string

A printed number carries its precision in its digits. "0.80" says two decimal places, "0.8" says one, and as floating-point numbers the two are identical. Once a printed value has been read in as a number, the comparison at printed precision can no longer be made, because the precision is gone.

We therefore stored every printed value as the string the page prints, in the extraction and in the committed ground truth, and compared strings: the computed value is formatted with the printed number of decimals (`sprintf("%.2f", x)` in R), and the two strings are compared after the clean-up below. A comparison by numeric tolerance fails in both directions. Too loose a tolerance passed a value that the row's own note said disagreed; values sitting exactly on a rounding boundary were reported as mismatches when they were not.

The string is easy to lose by accident. A CSV reader that guesses column types will read a column of numeric-looking strings as numbers, turning "0.020" into 0.02 and "-0.00" into 0. We forced the column type to character everywhere the printed value is read, and checked that the file on disk still stores the string, since a script can carry the string internally and then write a number at the end.

## Clean-up before comparing

Both sides get the same treatment:

- restore a missing leading zero (".23" becomes "0.23");
- replace a typographic minus sign with a hyphen;
- remove thousands separators;
- treat a negative zero as zero.

A tolerance of `1e-9` absorbs floating-point representation, and nothing else.

## Rounding errors are errors

A value rounded the wrong way at the printed precision is an erratum. The text that prints 0.23 for a value of 0.2230 is wrong at the precision it chose, and so is a value truncated rather than rounded (0.699 printed for 0.6996). These errata are small, and most of them are hand-typed numbers in the body text, where nothing generated them from the code.

The computed side must be compared at full precision. If the rewrite stores a value already rounded (an R-squared kept as 0.0115) and that value is rounded again for comparison, the result can disagree with the page (0.011 against a printed 0.012) when the full-precision value (0.01150090) agrees. Every table in the rewrite is written unrounded beside its formatted version for this reason.

## Hedged numbers

When the sentence itself hedges, we compared within half a step of the sentence's own precision. We treated the following words as hedges: "approximately", "about", "roughly", "around", "nearly", "close to", "on the order of".

- "about 37" tolerates 36.5 to 37.5;
- "about 40 percent" tolerates 35 to 45 percent.

A hedge needs that bound. Our first version of the rule simply returned no verdict for a hedged number, and it hid one paper's largest error: an appendix said one effect was "about 37 percentage points" when the estimate was 29.7, and the hedge exempted it from every check. A hedge excuses a rounding difference, not an arbitrary one.

The hedge has to be on the page. A sentence that states a bare figure or a bare interval asserts it exactly, and the fact that the true value is close is not a defence. An effect described as running "between 0.30 and 0.50 standard deviations", about estimates of 0.283 and 0.522, is an erratum, even though both estimates round to the endpoints at one decimal place.

## Differences of printed cells

When the text reports a difference between two printed values, each value was rounded on its own, so the difference can legitimately be off by one unit in the last printed digit. We allowed exactly that, with the tolerance set slightly wider than one unit so that it never sits on a floating-point boundary. Without that margin, a gap of exactly one unit can fail: 0.8 minus 0.7 computes as 0.10000000000000009, which is not at most 0.1.

## The archive's precision

The deposited code often prints its own output at a fixed precision (a tibble shows three significant digits, a Stata log a few decimals). The archive's value is compared at the coarser of the page's precision and the precision the deposited code printed. Any finer comparison manufactures disagreement between two numbers that agree as far as either was ever printed.

Sometimes rounding twice is the deposit's own convention: a table that rounds to three places and then formats to two prints 0.55 for a rate of 0.5449. The rewrite declines to round twice and computes 0.54, while the archive reproduces the page exactly. We recorded both values and explained in the notes which was which, so that the rewrite's choice did not read as a failure to reproduce.


<!-- file: rules/stochastic.md -->

# Numbers that come from random draws

Bootstrap intervals, randomization-inference p-values, simulated power, permutation tests, and anything else built on random draws can print a different number on every run. A difference between such a number and the page is not, by itself, evidence of an error. It is not evidence of no error either, and the rule below exists to keep the second mistake from hiding behind the first.

## First, confirm that something draws

Before putting a difference down to randomness, we checked that the procedure actually draws at random. A `set.seed()` call at the top of a script is not evidence of that. One paper set a seed twice and never drew a random number; its results were identical at any seed. An earlier pass had explained a real mismatch in that paper as bootstrap noise from a function that, on inspection, uses the jackknife, which is deterministic. More than once, a difference that looked like noise was a bug.

The check is cheap: run the procedure at two or three very different seeds. If nothing moves, nothing draws, and the difference needs another explanation.

## Seeded procedures

When the deposited code sets a seed, the archive check in [Stage 1](../stages/01_archive_check.md) tries to reproduce the printed value exactly, under the software of the paper's day. For R, the date that matters most is April 2019: R 3.6.0 changed the default algorithm behind `sample()`, so code that draws with `sample()` and was run before then needs `RNGkind(sample.kind = "Rounding")` to reproduce its own output. We tested the old sampler before concluding that a seeded archive was broken, and it often turned out not to be.

The maintained rewrite keeps the current sampler, because it is the code we would write now. Where the current sampler moves a published number, the ground truth records `defect_locus = environment`. Neither the paper nor the archive is wrong; the software changed underneath them.

Two practical notes. Setting the sampler inside a script and expecting `on.exit()` to restore it does not work reliably when scripts are sourced in sequence from `run_all.R`, so we restored it explicitly and asserted the result. A published number should also be checked under the conditions of the document that printed it: a corrigendum published years after the article may have been computed with different software, or different inputs, from the article it corrects.

## Unseeded procedures

When the deposited code sets no seed, the printed value is a single unlabelled draw, and no run can be expected to match it. We reran the procedure across many seeds (a few hundred was usually enough) and asked whether the printed value was consistent with the resulting distribution. Two illustrations:

- A chi-squared p-value ran from 0.0005 to 0.004 over 500 replications, and about a quarter of the draws rounded to the printed value. The printed value holds.
- The endpoints of a simulated interval were printed as $1.70 and $13.71. Over 200 seeds the endpoints ranged from $1.66 to $1.73 and from $11.79 to $15.19. Both printed values hold.

A printed value far outside any reasonable draw is an erratum. A printed value inside the distribution is not, even when no single run reproduces it.

In the ground truth, such a row leaves `match_rewrite` empty, since there is no single value to match, and records the verdict in `holds`. Filling in `match_rewrite = TRUE` beside a `value_rewrite` that visibly differs would make the row contradict itself. The same encoding applies whatever the claim type: a `pipeline` claim whose printed value comes from an unseeded procedure needs it just as much as a `descriptive` one.

## Unseeded figures

The same problem arises in figures, where it is easier to miss. A figure whose layout depends on random draws (a jittered scatter, simulated intervals, labels placed by a stochastic algorithm) can change with every run. In one paper with no seed, 9 of 20 seeds moved at least one published label. The archive runs without error and still cannot reproduce its own figure, even in principle. Where we found this, we measured how much the figure moved at the printed precision and reported it, rather than calling the figure reproduced or not.

## In the errata

A value inside the distribution is not an erratum and does not appear in the note. Where such a row carries a locus anyway (a seeded value that the current sampler moves, say, but only within the range over seeds), its disposition is `documented_only`, with the range as the reason. A value far outside the distribution is an ordinary erratum, and its corrected value is computed from the rewrite in the usual way, with the seed recorded so that the correction itself reproduces.


<!-- file: rules/severity.md -->

# Which errors go to the journal

Active maintenance finds errors in bulk, and nearly all of them are trivial: a 2.9 that should have been a 3.0, panels of a figure in the wrong order, a misspelled name in a reference. The scientific contribution of the paper stands without the fix. A few are not trivial. This page describes how we decided which was which, and what we did with each.

## Three tiers

1. **Every error goes in the errata note**, beside the maintained code, where anyone reading the repository will find it. The note is public, itemized, and computed from the code (see [Stage 5](../stages/05_errata.md)).
2. **An error that changes the direction or implications of a finding a reader would rely on also goes to the journal**, as a corrigendum. In our experience these are rare.
3. **Retraction is for findings that can no longer be relied on at all.**

## Why not send everything

Sending every author's list of small corrections to every journal would bury the editors in notices that change nothing a reader would act on. A corrigendum is a signal that something important changed. Spent on typos and rounding slips, it stops being one. The errata note takes the volume, so that the journal notice can carry the weight.

## Where the line comes from

Existing policies say a good deal about the line between correction and retraction and little about the line between a corrigendum and no notice at all. We borrowed from both ends. The Committee on Publication Ethics reserves retraction for articles whose findings and conclusions cannot be relied upon, whatever the cause. Some medical journals ask for only a correction, even for pervasive errors, when the errors do not change the direction or implications of the results. Our second tier takes that phrase and applies it one level down: an error that changes the direction or implications of a finding warrants a notice in the journal, and one that does not can live in the errata.

## The abstract is not the test

It is tempting to send a corrigendum only for errors that touch the abstract. We did not use that test. The first error we sent to a journal concerned a persistence claim: the paper said the effect of fact-checks on factual beliefs was still detectable more than two weeks later at half its original size, and the corrected estimate was about a third of the original and could not be distinguished from zero. The claim was not the paper's central finding and was not in the abstract. The article made it three times in the main text, though, and the durability of fact-checking effects is a question readers of that literature care about. A reader could rely on it, so it went to the journal.

## When a corrigendum goes, related errors go with it

Once a corrigendum was warranted, we used it to correct the related errors in the same article too, so that the published record and the errata note do not disagree. Unrelated trivial errors stayed in the note.

## Errors an earlier correction already fixed

Some errors had been corrected already, by a corrigendum published years before. Those are recorded with `disposition = corrected_by_journal`. Reading the article against the old corrigendum also turned up sentences that went on restating a finding the corrigendum had withdrawn. Each of those sentences is an erratum of its own, and they went into the note.

## Who decides

Whether an error changes a conclusion is a judgment the pipeline cannot make. The agent drafted the errata and flagged the candidates; the author decided, and for anything sent to a journal the coauthors decided together. When an entry changes a conclusion, the errata note says so at the top.

## How the tiers appear in the data

The `disposition` column of the ground truth records what happened to each error ([Stage 2](../stages/02_ground_truth.md)):

| `disposition` | Tier |
|---|---|
| `corrected_here` | Tier 1: an entry in this repository's errata corrects it. Computed from the errata, never typed. |
| `corrected_by_journal` | Tier 2 (or an earlier correction): a published corrigendum or erratum corrects it. |
| `documented_only` | Recorded and deliberately not corrected, such as a value within simulation noise or an archive bug that never reached the page. |
| `not_corrected` | Known, and left uncorrected for a stated reason. |

Every error in the printed text must have a disposition before the build passes, since an error nobody has decided about is unfinished.


<!-- file: schemas/README.md -->

# Schemas

Every paper's repository produces the same seven tables, with the same columns in the same order. We settled on one schema for all of them after finding that repositories built months apart had drifted into different column names for the same thing, which made it impossible to summarize the collection without a translation layer for each paper.

| Table | Path | Written in | Schema |
|---|---|---|---|
| Deposit manifest | `original_manifest.csv` | [Stage 1](../stages/01_archive_check.md) | [`original_manifest.md`](original_manifest.md) |
| Archive run | `ground_truth/archive_run_status.csv` | [Stage 1](../stages/01_archive_check.md) | [`archive_run_status.md`](archive_run_status.md) |
| Archive overwrites | `ground_truth/archive_overwrites.csv` | [Stage 1](../stages/01_archive_check.md) | [`archive_overwrites.md`](archive_overwrites.md) |
| Claims extraction | `ground_truth/published_claims.csv` | [Stage 4](../stages/04_claims.md) | [`published_claims.md`](published_claims.md) |
| Ground truth | `ground_truth/<paper_id>_ground_truth.csv` | [Stage 2](../stages/02_ground_truth.md) | [`ground_truth.md`](ground_truth.md) |
| Float coverage | `ground_truth/float_coverage.csv` | [Stage 2](../stages/02_ground_truth.md) | [`float_coverage.md`](float_coverage.md) |
| Errata | `errata_entries.csv` | [Stage 5](../stages/05_errata.md) | [`errata_entries.md`](errata_entries.md) |

## Conventions that apply to every table

- **The tables are build output.** Each is written by a script in the repository, and a change is made by changing the script, never by editing the CSV. The two exceptions are the printed values and the claim classifications in `published_claims.csv`, which a person transcribes and reviews; even there, the file is read by code and never edited to make a check pass.
- **Every table exists in every repository.** A deposit that could not be run still gets an `archive_run_status.csv` saying why, and an `archive_overwrites.csv` with a header and no rows. A paper with no tables or figures gets a header-only `float_coverage.csv`. A missing file is then always a failure, never a sign that a stage did not apply.
- **Logical columns are written `TRUE`, `FALSE`, or `NA`**, never `1` and `0`, and never left as an empty string where `NA` is meant.
- **Printed values are text.** Any column that holds a number as the page prints it (`value_paper`, `published`) is stored as the string, so that the precision survives. See [`rules/rounding.md`](../rules/rounding.md).
- **Floats are named as printed**: `Table 1`, `Figure B.2`, never `table_1`.
- **Closed vocabularies are closed.** Each schema page lists the allowed values for its categorical columns, and the build rejects anything else. A value that seems to need a new category usually means the row has been misclassified.

## Older names

If you are migrating an older repository, the main renames were `table_figure` to `location`, `operator` to `comparison`, and a handful of archive tables (`archive_script_status.csv`, `archive_generated_files.csv`, and others) folded into `archive_run_status.csv` and `archive_overwrites.csv`. Archive pass names such as `deposited` and `as_deposited` became `as_shipped`, and `clean` became `stripped`. Columns that only one repository carried were folded into `notes` or dropped.


<!-- file: schemas/original_manifest.md -->

# `original_manifest.csv`

One row per file in the replication deposit. The manifest is the repository's record of what the deposit held, and `download_original.R` checks every download against it ([Stage 1](../stages/01_archive_check.md)). We built each manifest from the archive's API rather than by hand.

The columns differ by archive, because the archives publish different things about each file.

## Dataverse

`file, directory_label, dataverse_file_id, file_persistent_id, bytes, md5_served, md5_published, unf, served_as`

| Column | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `file` | text | The file's original name, as the authors uploaded it. |
| `directory_label` | text | The folder the file sits in within the deposit; empty for a file at the top level. |
| `dataverse_file_id` | integer | Dataverse's numeric file id, used to download it. |
| `file_persistent_id` | text | The file's own DOI, where the installation assigns one; empty otherwise. |
| `bytes` | integer | Size of the original file in bytes. |
| `md5_served` | text | MD5 of the bytes the download actually returns. |
| `md5_published` | text | MD5 that Dataverse publishes in the file's metadata. |
| `unf` | text | Dataverse's Universal Numerical Fingerprint, for tabular files it has ingested; empty otherwise. |
| `served_as` | text | The file name the download returns. |

`md5_served` and `md5_published` usually agree. They part when Dataverse has ingested a tabular upload (a `.dta` or `.csv`, say) and serves its own `.tab` version by default: the published checksum describes the original upload and the served bytes are the conversion. We downloaded with `?format=original` so that the original is what arrives, and recorded both checksums so that a disagreement is visible rather than silent.

## OSF

`file, directory_label, osf_file_id, bytes, md5_served, md5_published, sha256_published`

| Column | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `file` | text | The file's name. |
| `directory_label` | text | The folder within the OSF storage; empty at the top level. |
| `osf_file_id` | text | OSF's id for the file. |
| `bytes` | integer | Size in bytes. |
| `md5_served` | text | MD5 of the bytes the download returns. |
| `md5_published` | text | MD5 that OSF publishes for the file. |
| `sha256_published` | text | SHA-256 that OSF publishes for the file. |

OSF stores one set of bytes and publishes two checksums of it, with no converted version, so the served-versus-published problem above cannot arise.

## Other archives

The rule that carries over: record every checksum the archive publishes, record the byte size, and have the download stop on any disagreement with an independent claim about the bytes.

## Checks

The download stops if a file's size or served checksum differs from the manifest, or if `original/` contains a file the manifest does not list (hidden files included). A disagreement with the published checksum is printed without stopping. Zip and RAR files are unpacked into their own folders and checked against a second manifest of their contents.


<!-- file: schemas/archive_run_status.md -->

# `ground_truth/archive_run_status.csv`

One row per deposited script per pass: what happened when we ran the archive ([Stage 1](../stages/01_archive_check.md)).

`pass, script, role, exit_status, outcome, stopped_at`

| Column | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `pass` | closed | Which copy of the deposit the script ran in. |
| `script` | text | The script's path within the deposit. |
| `role` | closed | What the script does. |
| `exit_status` | integer | The process exit status; `0` is success, `NA` if the script was not run. |
| `outcome` | closed | How the run ended. |
| `stopped_at` | text | The error message (or the first lines of it) where the script stopped; for `not_run`, the reason it was not run; `NA` for a clean run. |

## Allowed values

**`pass`**

| Value | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `as_shipped` | The deposit exactly as downloaded, intermediate files and all. |
| `stripped` | Only the raw data and the code, with every intermediate file the deposit shipped removed, so that each script has to rebuild what it reads. |

The table is long: a script run in both passes has two rows.

**`role`**

| Value | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `cleaning` | Turns raw data into analysis data. |
| `analysis` | Produces tables, figures, or reported numbers. |
| `other` | Anything else the deposit runs directly. |

A helper file that is only ever sourced by other scripts gets no row, since it never runs on its own.

**`outcome`**

| Value | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `clean` | Ran to the end without error. |
| `error` | Stopped with an error. |
| `timeout` | Did not finish in the time allowed. |
| `not_run` | Not run, for a reason given in `stopped_at` (it needs Stata, say, or a proprietary dataset). |

## What this table does not say

`clean` means the script ran. Whether it reproduced the paper's numbers is a separate question, answered by the ground truth. A script can run cleanly and reproduce nothing, and a script that errors halfway through can still have printed the numbers we needed. The table answers the first question only.

A deposit we could not run at all still writes this table, with one `not_run` row per script.


<!-- file: schemas/archive_overwrites.md -->

# `ground_truth/archive_overwrites.csv`

One row per file that running the archive created, changed, or removed, in either pass ([Stage 1](../stages/01_archive_check.md)). We found these by comparing every file's checksum and modification time with the manifest after each run.

`pass, file, effect, matches_deposit`

| Column | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `pass` | closed | `as_shipped` or `stripped`, as in [`archive_run_status.md`](archive_run_status.md). |
| `file` | text | The file's path within the deposit. |
| `effect` | closed | What the run did to the file. |
| `matches_deposit` | logical | Whether the file the run wrote is byte-identical to the deposited one; `NA` for an added or withheld file, which has nothing to compare with. |

## Allowed values of `effect`

| Value | Pass | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `added` | either | The run wrote a file the deposit does not contain. |
| `overwritten` | `as_shipped` | The run rewrote a file the deposit shipped. |
| `rebuilt` | `stripped` | The run regenerated an intermediate file that had been removed for the stripped pass. |
| `withheld` | `stripped` | An intermediate file removed for the stripped pass that the run did not rebuild. |
| `deleted` | either | The run removed a deposited file. |

## Reading it

`overwritten` or `rebuilt` with `matches_deposit = FALSE` is the informative row. It means the deposited code, run today, does not produce the file the authors deposited: either the deposited file came from different code than the code that was deposited, or the software has moved since. The ground truth then has to say which ([Stage 2](../stages/02_ground_truth.md)).

`withheld` marks an intermediate that no deposited script produces. Any script that reads it can only run in the as-shipped pass, which leans on a file nobody can regenerate.

A deposit that could not be run writes this table with a header and no rows.


<!-- file: schemas/published_claims.md -->

# `ground_truth/published_claims.csv`

The extraction: one row per claim the article and its appendix make, numeric or not ([Stage 4](../stages/04_claims.md)). Unlike the other tables, much of this one is transcribed by a person: the printed values and the classifications are read off the page.
