It is reviewed by hand, committed, and read by both the ground truth build and `in_text_claims.R`.

`claim_id, location, claim_type, claim, value_paper, digits, comparison, expect, needs_block, notes`

| Column | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `claim_id` | text | A unique, readable id (`t1_mturk_within`, `disc_spillover_ratio`). The key that joins this table to the ground truth, the claims script, and the errata. |
| `location` | text | Where the claim is printed: a float (`Table 1`), a page and section, a footnote, or an appendix section. |
| `claim_type` | closed | What kind of claim it is. |
| `claim` | text | A short description of what the number or statement is, including its units. |
| `value_paper` | text | The value as printed, normalized only in typography (leading zero, minus sign, thousands separators). For a claim with no number, the statement's truth value. |
| `digits` | integer | The number of decimal places the page prints. A `descriptive` claim has `0`. |
| `comparison` | closed | How the printed value relates to the quantity. |
| `expect` | closed | The non-default verdict the claims script declares for this claim, if any. |
| `needs_block` | logical | Whether `in_text_claims.R` must have a block for this claim. |
| `notes` | text | Anything a reader needs to interpret the row. |

## Allowed values

**`claim_type`**

| Value | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `pipeline` | A number the analysis produces: an estimate, a standard error, a p-value, a sample size. |
| `descriptive` | A claim about the results, often with no number: significance, direction, order, persistence. |
| `definitional` | A number that defines the design: the number of arms, a scale's range, a wave's date. |
| `structural` | A number about the document itself: "three experiments", the number of rows in a table. |
| `transcribed` | A number quoted from another source, such as another study's estimate. |

**`comparison`**

| Value | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `==` | The printed value is the quantity, at the printed precision. The default for every row with a `value_paper`. |
| `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=` | The sentence states a bound ("less than 5 percent"). |
| `approx` | The sentence hedges the number ("about", "roughly"). The hedge's tolerance is set in [`rules/rounding.md`](../rules/rounding.md). |
| `NA` | The row has no `value_paper`. |

**`expect`**: `NA` (the usual case: the check compares values), `range`, `derived`, `shape`, or `absent`. The meanings are the verdicts of the same names in [Stage 4](../stages/04_claims.md). The column records what the claims script declares; the script, not this column, is what decides.

## Rules

- `needs_block` is `TRUE` for every `pipeline` and `descriptive` claim, and for any `definitional` or `structural` claim the pipeline can actually reach. The claims script must print exactly the claims marked `TRUE`, no more and no fewer.
- `digits` lives here and nowhere else. Both instruments read it from this file, so they cannot disagree about a claim's precision. The build also checks that `value_paper`, formatted at `digits`, gives back the stored string, which catches a wrong precision that would otherwise pass on both sides.
- `value_paper` is read as text. A CSV reader left to guess will turn "0.020" into 0.02.
- `claim_type` is the boundary of what gets checked, and nothing downstream audits it. We compared the `descriptive` and `definitional` rows within each section by hand, because the same construction, classified two ways two paragraphs apart, once left one of a pair of identical errors uncaught.


<!-- file: schemas/ground_truth.md -->

# `ground_truth/<paper_id>_ground_truth.csv`

One row per printed value or claim checked against the code: every cell of every table, every plotted quantity we could count, and every `pipeline` and `descriptive` claim in the text ([Stage 2](../stages/02_ground_truth.md)). The table is built by `ground_truth/build_ground_truth.R` as the last step of `run_all.R`, and the only values typed into it are the printed ones.

`paper_id, claim_id, location, claim_type, claim, value_paper, digits, value_script, match, value_rewrite, match_rewrite, holds, defect_locus, disposition, disposition_reason, notes`

| Column | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `paper_id` | text | The paper's id, the same on every row. |
| `claim_id` | text | The key into `published_claims.csv`. Table cells, which have no extraction row, get ids of their own. |
| `location` | text | Taken from the extraction where the claim is there; a float cell keeps the float's name. |
| `claim_type` | closed | Copied from the extraction, so that the table reads on its own; float cells are `pipeline`. |
| `claim` | text | What the value is. |
| `value_paper` | text | The printed value, as a string. |
| `digits` | integer | The printed precision. From the extraction where the claim is there; for a float cell, from the printed string. |
| `value_script` | number | The value the deposited code produces, recovered from the Stage 1 run; `NA` where the archive was not run or does not produce it. |
| `match` | logical | Whether `value_script` agrees with `value_paper`, compared at the coarser of the page's precision and the precision the deposited code prints. |
| `value_rewrite` | number | The value the maintained rewrite produces, read from `maintained/output/` at full precision. |
| `match_rewrite` | logical | Whether `value_rewrite` agrees with `value_paper` at the printed precision; `NA` for an unseeded value, where no single run can match. |
| `holds` | logical | For a claim that is a statement rather than a value (a `descriptive` claim, or an unseeded value judged against its distribution), whether it is true of the rewrite's output. |
| `defect_locus` | closed | Where the problem lies, on every row where a comparison fails. |
| `disposition` | closed | What was done about the problem. |
| `disposition_reason` | text | Why, for the three dispositions that are judgments. |
| `notes` | text | Anything else, including a second contributing cause. |

The rules for comparing a computed value with a printed one are in [`rules/rounding.md`](../rules/rounding.md), and for values from random draws in [`rules/stochastic.md`](../rules/stochastic.md).

## Allowed values

**`claim_type`**: `pipeline`, `descriptive`, `definitional`, `structural`, `transcribed`, as in [`published_claims.md`](published_claims.md).

**`defect_locus`**

| Value | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `paper_internal` | The printed text is wrong: the code produces one number and the page prints another. |
| `archive` | The deposited code is wrong, and the page printed what it produced. |
| `environment` | The software changed: the deposited code, run today, gives a different number than it did then. |
| `rewrite` | The rewrite is wrong. We fixed these, so none should remain. |
| `upstream` | The problem is in something the paper relied on, such as a dataset or an estimate it reused. |
| `unresolved` | We looked and could not tell. |
| `NA` | No defect. |

**`disposition`**

| Value | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `corrected_here` | An entry in this repository's errata corrects it. Computed from `errata_entries.csv`, never typed. |
| `corrected_by_journal` | A published corrigendum or erratum corrects it. |
| `documented_only` | Recorded and deliberately not corrected: a value within simulation noise, or an archive bug the rewrite repairs that never reached the page. |
| `not_corrected` | Known, and left uncorrected for a stated reason. |
| `NA` | Nobody has decided yet. |

How the dispositions map onto the decision about which errors go to a journal is in [`rules/severity.md`](../rules/severity.md).

## Rules the build enforces

- **The locus rule.** A row where `match`, `match_rewrite`, or `holds` is `FALSE` must have a `defect_locus`. A row where every comparison passes must not, with one exception: a bug the deposited code has, the page printed, and the rewrite at first reproduced, which an erratum names. Such a row carries `archive` despite matching everywhere. A row with no verdict at all may or may not carry a locus. The locus is set where each row is built, never as a default for the whole table.
- **Disposition follows locus.** Every row with a locus gets a disposition, or `NA` while undecided. The build stops on any `paper_internal` row whose disposition is `NA`; the other loci are reported as a count.
- **The printed values are the only typed values.** `value_script`, `value_rewrite`, every verdict, and `corrected_here` come from code. A typed number that agrees with a note is indistinguishable from a computed number that agrees with the data, and only the second is evidence.
- **Built from the article first.** The rows come from what the paper prints, joined to what the pipeline produces, so that a printed value with no pipeline counterpart shows up as a row with an empty `value_rewrite` rather than not at all.
- **Joins are checked in both directions.** Every join asserts that its keys are unique on both sides and that the result is one-to-one, since a join that silently matches nothing looks the same as a table with nothing wrong.
- **Rows are never selected by their printed value.** Filtering pipeline output for the number the page prints guarantees a match.


<!-- file: schemas/float_coverage.md -->

# `ground_truth/float_coverage.csv`

One row per table and figure in the article and appendix, saying how much of each the ground truth actually checks ([Stage 2](../stages/02_ground_truth.md)). We added it after a coverage check that asked only whether each float had at least one row passed for months on a figure with one checked value out of more than a hundred printed.

`float, published_numbers, covered, reproduced_by_rewrite, reproduced_by_archive, plotted, plotted_reproduced, note`

| Column | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `float` | text | The float's name as printed (`Table 2`, `Figure B.3`). |
| `published_numbers` | integer | The numbers printed on the float: every cell of a table, and any numbers printed on the face of a figure. |
| `covered` | integer | How many of those numbers have a row in the ground truth. |
| `reproduced_by_rewrite` | integer | How many of the covered numbers the rewrite reproduces. |
| `reproduced_by_archive` | integer | How many of the covered numbers the deposited code reproduces. |
| `plotted` | integer | For a figure, the number of plotted quantities (points, bars, interval endpoints); `NA` for a table. |
| `plotted_reproduced` | integer | How many plotted quantities the rewrite reproduces; `NA` for a table. |
| `note` | text | Anything a count needs, such as why a float carries no data. |

## Rules

- **The list of floats comes from the article,** not from the scripts. An article's own front matter or numbering says what it contains, and the table is checked against that list, so a float with no script still gets a row.
- **A figure that prints no numbers is not thereby covered.** Its `published_numbers` is `0`, and what it plots is the claim, so `plotted` and `plotted_reproduced` carry the check. A figure is never passed just because it prints no numbers.
- **Some figures cannot be counted.** A figure with too many points to count records what the rewrite plots and says so in `note`; a continuous surface records that it has no discrete points. A diagram that carries no data gets zero counts and a `note`.
- **Every count is computed.** A typed count once sat a few lines below the code that should have produced it, and claimed eleven covered values where there were three.
- **The README states each fraction.** Computing coverage inside a check that only stops the build leaves a reader with nothing; the report reads this table and prints it.

A paper with no tables or figures writes this table with a header and no rows.


<!-- file: schemas/errata_entries.md -->

# `errata_entries.csv`

One row per entry in the errata note. `errata.qmd` writes this table when it renders the note, so the table and the PDF always say the same thing ([Stage 5](../stages/05_errata.md)).

`entry, class, source, form, title, location, published, corrected, note, claim_ids, corrected_values, values_in_spans`

| Column | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `entry` | integer | The entry's number in the note. Numbered by severity at first publication, then append-only. |
| `class` | closed | What kind of error it is. |
| `source` | closed | How we found it. |
| `form` | closed | How the note presents it. |
| `title` | text | A short heading for the entry. |
| `location` | text | Where the error is printed: main text, a section, a float, a footnote, an appendix section, or the references. |
| `published` | text | The passage as printed, with each changed span marked `[[like this]]`. |
| `corrected` | text | The passage as it should read, with the same spans marked. Corrected values in it are computed when the note renders. |
| `note` | text | The explanation: what was wrong, why, and what the correction rests on. |
| `claim_ids` | text | The ground-truth and extraction rows the entry corrects, separated by semicolons; empty for an entry with no row. |
| `corrected_values` | text | One corrected value per id in `claim_ids`, in the same order, separated by semicolons. Only `quantity` entries carry them. |
| `values_in_spans` | logical | `TRUE` when every corrected value is the token the corrected sentence prints; `FALSE` when a value is stored on the claim's scale rather than the sentence's (a proportion printed as a percentage, say); `NA` for an entry with no values. |

## Allowed values

**`class`**

| Value | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `quantity` | A wrong number. |
| `description` | A method, sample, or variable described differently from what was done. |
| `interpretation` | A conclusion that does not follow once the estimates are corrected. |
| `definition` | A wrong definition, display, or proof step. |
| `label` | A wrong axis label, legend, or panel title. |
| `float` | A float that is wrong as a whole, such as panels in the wrong order. |
| `cross_reference` | A pointer to the wrong table, figure, or section. |
| `wording` | A wrong word that changes no number or substance. |
| `spelling` | A misspelling, including of a name. |
| `typography` | A typesetting error. |
| `bibliographic` | An error in the reference list. |

**`source`**

| Value | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `pipeline` | The rewrite computed a different value. |
| `reading` | Reading the article against itself, its appendix, and its code. |
| `reference_audit` | Checking every reference against Crossref. |
| `publisher_record` | An earlier published correction. |
| `authors_archive` | The authors' own files outside the deposit. |
| `proof` | The proofs or the accepted manuscript. |

**`form`**

| Value | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `full` | The published and corrected passages, quoted in full. |
| `brief` | A one-line correction. |
| `note` | An explanation with no replacement text. |

## Checks the render runs

- Every id in `claim_ids` exists in the ground truth or the extraction.
- Only `quantity` entries carry `corrected_values`, and there is one value per id.
- Every corrected value appears in the corrected passage (or `values_in_spans` says why not).
- No corrected value renders identically to the published one at the printed precision, since then there is nothing to correct.
- No entry corrects a claim the pipeline reproduces.
- Every quotation in `published` has been checked against an image of the printed page.

The ground truth's `corrected_here` disposition is computed from `claim_ids`, which is why this table carries them.


<!-- file: traps.md -->

# Traps

The failures we hit more than once, or hit once at real cost, with what we did about them. Most are silent: the code runs, the checks pass, and the answer is wrong. They are grouped by the stage where they bite. The examples are R, because our code was R; the shapes carry over to any language (see [`languages.md`](languages.md)).

## Fetching and running the archive

- **Running the archive in place.** A deposited script that saves a figure to a bare relative path overwrote a file the deposit ships, so the working copy no longer matched the archive, and the checksum check passed only because it had run first. Run every deposited script in a scratch copy, never in the downloaded folder.
- **Write calls split across lines.** A search for code that writes files misses a `write.csv(` whose file argument is on the next line. Join continued lines before searching.
- **Shipped intermediates.** A script ran cleanly against the deposit as downloaded while the script that should have produced its input had failed; it was reading the deposited copy. One deposit went from "four of six scripts run" to "five of six fail" once its intermediates were removed. Run a second pass on a copy stripped to raw data and code ([`schemas/archive_run_status.md`](schemas/archive_run_status.md)).
- **The archive that runs and writes nothing.** One deposit had every write commented out, so it ran without error and left nothing to compare. A clean exit is not evidence of anything; check what the run produced.
- **Printing nothing.** In R, `source()` prints nothing unless told to (`print.eval = TRUE`), so a harness that sources the deposited scripts records exit statuses correctly while capturing an empty log. We concluded that no archive values were recoverable from one paper until we turned printing on and recovered over a hundred. A deposit that builds a table object and comments out the print call can still be made to print it.
- **A single container file.** When the deposit is one zip or RAR, the "no unlisted files" check runs on a folder holding one file and checks nothing. Unpack into a folder of its own and check the members against a second manifest.
- **A reason for skipping work that was never tested.** We skipped one analysis because its package was "unmaintained"; it had been updated the day before, and installing it surfaced the paper's only real reproducibility failure. Three other packages we had recorded as removed turned out to install and run. Test the reason before accepting it.

## Software that changed underneath the code

- **Dispatch drift.** A test function from one package, given a model fit from another, used to fall through to a classical test. A later version of the second package added the method it was looking for, and the identical line began returning a robust test: 17 of 18 cells in one table moved, with no error or warning. Nothing but comparison with the printed numbers catches this. Expect it wherever deposited code combines two packages.
- **A package that changes another package on load.** Loading one package replaced fourteen functions in base R and `stats`, and broke an unrelated package's estimator for the rest of the session. To find such a package, record every function in the loaded namespaces, attach the deposit's packages one at a time, and see which attach changes something. Bisecting by the failure finds only the first culprit.
- **The random-number sampler.** R 3.6.0 changed how `sample()` draws. Seeded code from before April 2019 needs `RNGkind(sample.kind = "Rounding")` to reproduce itself ([`rules/stochastic.md`](rules/stochastic.md)), and the setting has to be restored explicitly afterwards, since `on.exit()` does not reliably restore it when scripts are sourced in sequence.
- **Sort order.** dplyr 1.1 sorts character keys in the C locale by default, which puts every capitalised word ahead of every lowercase one. Every value stayed correct and the rows moved, and a cell-by-cell comparison against the published table reported 172 of 717 cells wrong when none were. Pass the locale explicitly, or compare by key rather than by position.
- **Weights that quietly disappear.** Refitting a weighted model from its own `model.frame()` drops the weights, which pairs weighted coefficients with unweighted standard errors; it moved one coefficient's sign. Pass the weights explicitly.

## Writing the rewrite

- **A modern equivalent that is not equivalent.** Replacing base R's `expand.grid()` with tidyr's `expand_grid()` transposed a grid, because the two vary their arguments in opposite orders. Every number still matched; only the figure was wrong, and it stayed wrong for months until someone laid the rendered figure beside the published one. Compare every figure by eye, as well as its numbers.
- **Factor order in a deposited data file.** A treatment variable stored as a factor whose first level was a treatment arm, not the control, reversed the sign of every contrast taken without releveling. The standard errors looked normal, the script ran cleanly and deterministically, and only the comparison with the published numbers caught it. Set the reference level explicitly.
- **A column name that shadows an argument.** A helper written `mutate(outcome = outcome)` on a table that already had an `outcome` column assigned the column to itself, so the labels were wrong while every cell was right, and a later filter silently dropped a whole experiment. Name arguments so they cannot collide with columns.
- **A script that skips its own work.** An `if (file.exists(out))` guard returns the committed output instead of recomputing it, so the run passes while the code may be broken ([Stage 3](stages/03_rewrite.md)).
- **An output file that exists is not a render that worked.** A loop that checked for `README.md` passed on stale files after a column rename had broken three reports. Check the exit status.
- **Unseeded draws.** A pipeline with an unseeded random draw gives a different answer on the second run, and nothing downstream means anything until it is fixed. Run everything twice and diff the outputs.

## Building the ground truth

- **The printed value read as a number.** A CSV reader that guesses types turns "0.80" into 0.8 and "-0.00" into 0, and the precision needed for the comparison is gone. Force the column to text, and check that the file on disk still stores the string ([`rules/rounding.md`](rules/rounding.md)).
- **Hand-typed comparison values.** A typed number that agrees with a note looks exactly like a computed number that agrees with the data. One repository had a typed coverage count of 11 a few lines below code that would have said 3. Generate everything except the printed values.
- **Selecting a row by the number you expect.** Filtering pipeline output for the value the page prints guarantees a match. Select by key.
- **Joins that match nothing.** A join on a column that was missing for two of the studies left 72 of 130 rows unmatched, and the table read as if nothing were wrong. Route every join through one helper that checks keys are unique on both sides and the result is one-to-one.
- **Building from the pipeline instead of the article.** A ground truth built from what the rewrite produces cannot see what the rewrite does not produce. One paper's first ground truth had 40 rows, all matching, covering little more than a third of the paper. Start from the printed page.
- **"At least one row per float."** A figure with one checked value out of more than a hundred printed passed that test for months. Report coverage as a fraction for each float ([`schemas/float_coverage.md`](schemas/float_coverage.md)).
- **Rounding a value before comparing it.** A value stored as 0.0115 rounds to 0.011, while the full-precision 0.01150090 rounds to the printed 0.012. Compare from full precision.

## Reading the published article

- **PDF text extraction.** Text pulled from a PDF changes characters silently. In one paper `=` came out as `5` and the minus sign as `2`, so a printed −1.5 arrived as 21.5. Multi-column regression tables were mis-aligned by a column, which produced a phantom erratum that survived two reviews. Check every quoted sentence and every transcribed cell against an image of the page, and read numbers printed on a figure by position rather than in reading order.
- **Numbers written as words.** A sweep for digits misses "five successive elections" and "in all but one study". Run a second pass for number words.
- **The preprint.** A preprint's numbers are not the published numbers. Transcribe from the published version.
- **Testing a document against the wrong materials.** A corrigendum restated one paper's original confidence intervals differently from the article's appendix. We first wrote that up as an error in the corrigendum. It was not: the corrigendum had redrawn the original analysis from its own working files, whose inputs differed, and on those inputs it was right. Check a printed number under the conditions of the document that printed it.


<!-- file: languages.md -->

# Languages other than R

> **Needs review.** Our code was R, so the R column below is what we used, and the Stata and Python columns are not. We drafted them from each language's documentation, not from running the procedure in it. If you work in Stata or Python and find something wrong or missing, please open an issue.

The procedure does not depend on R. What it needs from a language is a short list of capabilities: build paths from the project root, run everything from one entry point, fix the random-number generator, compute the paper's standard errors, write unrounded output beside every table and figure, verify downloads by checksum, read printed values as text, and format a number at a given precision. This page maps each one.

## Counterparts

| Need | R (what we used) | Stata | Python |
|---|---|---|---|
| Paths from the project root | `here::here()`, anchored by `here::i_am()` | A global set once in the master do-file (`global root "..."`), with every path built from it; no `cd` inside scripts | `pathlib.Path`, anchored at the repository root (for example with `pyprojroot`) |
| One entry point that stops at the first failure | `run_all.R`, sourcing scripts in order | A master `.do` file calling each script with `do`; Stata stops on the first error unless told otherwise | `run_all.py` calling each step with `subprocess.run(..., check=True)`, or a `Makefile` |
| Fixed package versions | `renv` lockfile | Ship the user-written commands in the repository and point `sysdir set PLUS` at them; set `version` at the top of the master file | A pinned lockfile (`requirements.txt` with exact versions, or `uv.lock`) |
| Seeds and the generator | `set.seed()`; `RNGkind(sample.kind = "Rounding")` to reproduce pre-3.6 draws | `set seed`; the generator depends on `version` (`version 13` and earlier give the old KISS generator, later versions Mersenne Twister); `set sortseed` for ties | `numpy.random.default_rng(seed)`, passed explicitly; the legacy `np.random.seed()` and the standard library's `random` keep separate global states |
| Robust standard errors | `estimatr::lm_robust()`, HC2 by default | `vce(robust)` is HC1; `vce(hc2)` and `vce(hc3)` exist for `regress`; `vce(cluster)` is CR1 | `statsmodels` `cov_type="HC2"` (or `HC1`, `HC3`); `cov_type="cluster"` for clustering |
| Unrounded table output | `write_csv()` of the estimates beside the formatted table | `export delimited` or `putexcel` from stored results, beside the `esttab` or `collect` table | `DataFrame.to_csv()` beside `to_latex()` |
| A CSV beside every figure | `write_csv()` of the plotted values next to `ggsave()` | `export delimited` of the plotted variables next to `graph export` | `to_csv()` of the plotted values next to `savefig()` |
| Deterministic figure files | Blank the PDF `CreationDate` and `ModDate` after writing | Check whether `graph export` embeds a date; if it does, compare the CSVs only | `savefig(..., metadata={"CreationDate": None})` for PDF |
| Downloads verified by checksum | `download_original.R`: `curl` then `tools::md5sum()` | `copy` the file, then shell out to a checksum tool; Stata's own `checksum` is a CRC, not MD5 | `requests` and `hashlib.md5()` / `hashlib.sha256()` |
| Printed values read as text | `read_csv(col_types = cols(value_paper = col_character()))` | `import delimited, stringcols(_all)` | `pd.read_csv(..., dtype=str, keep_default_na=False)` |
| A number at the printed precision | `sprintf("%.2f", x)` | `string(x, "%9.2f")` (then trim) | `f"{x:.2f}"` |
| The claims check | `excheckr` | Not yet written | Not yet written |

Two cautions about the table.

**Default standard errors differ across languages.** Stata's `robust` is HC1, `estimatr`'s default is HC2, and `statsmodels` makes you choose. A rewrite in a different language from the original, or a port between packages in the same language, can move every standard error in a paper without anything being wrong in the code. The rewrite keeps the paper's estimator ([Stage 3](stages/03_rewrite.md)), which includes its variance estimator.

**Use the formatting function, not a rounding function.** Rounding functions differ on exact halves across languages (and some round half to even), while a format string applied to the full-precision value is what produces the digits the comparison needs. Whatever you use, test it on values that sit on a rounding boundary.

## The claims check

[Stage 4](stages/04_claims.md) describes the verdicts. Rewriting the check in another language means reproducing this behaviour; `excheckr` is one implementation of it, not the definition.

For each claim in `published_claims.csv` with `needs_block = TRUE`, a block in the claims script computes a value from the rewrite's output and declares it with the claim's id and, where the claim needs one, an expectation (`range`, `derived`, `shape`, or `absent`). The check looks up the claim's printed value and precision in the extraction, and the corrected value from any errata entry whose `claim_ids` name it. It formats the computed value at the printed precision, normalizing a negative zero, and then takes the first verdict that applies:

1. The block produced no value: `absent` if it declared `absent`, otherwise `MISSING`. (A block that declares `absent` and then produces a value is an error in the script, not a verdict.)
2. The block declared `range`, `derived`, or `shape`: that verdict. The declaration is the block's own statement that it has tested the condition, so the block's code must do the testing.
3. The claim has no printed value: `shape`.
4. An erratum corrects the claim: `STALE` if the computed value agrees with the printed value (the pipeline reproduces what the erratum says is wrong), `DRIFT` if it agrees with neither the printed nor the corrected value, and `corrected` if it agrees with the corrected value.
5. The computed value agrees with the printed value at the printed precision: `match`.
6. The claim's type is `descriptive`: `hedged`.
7. Otherwise: `MISMATCH`.

Each claim prints one line: `CLAIM <claim_id> = <computed value> || [verdict] <label>`. At the end the check prints a summary counting each verdict and stops with an error on any `MISMATCH`, `STALE`, `DRIFT`, or `MISSING`. Two counts are checked separately: the claims printed must be exactly the claims with `needs_block = TRUE`, and every claim that a `quantity` erratum names must score `corrected`.

`excheckr` also has an optional band for values from simulations: a failing value within a stated distance of its target scores `MEDIUM` and passes. Whether to carry that over depends on how your rewrite handles the cases in [`rules/stochastic.md`](rules/stochastic.md).

## Traps specific to Stata and Python

These are well-known hazards of each language rather than things we hit ourselves; they belong in [`traps.md`](traps.md) once someone has met them in practice.

**Stata**

- `sort` is not stable: observations with tied keys come out in an order that depends on the sort seed. Code that relies on the order of ties (taking the first observation in a group, say) can give different answers from run to run. Use `sort, stable` or break the ties.
- A missing numeric value is larger than every number, so `if x > 5` includes missing values.
- `generate` creates a 4-byte `float` by default, so `x == 0.1` can be false for a variable assigned 0.1. Use `double` (or `set type double`) for anything compared or reported.
- `merge m:m` does not do what its name suggests; it pairs observations by order within groups. Use `joinby` for a many-to-many join, and check `_merge` after every merge.
- `version` changes behaviour well beyond the random-number generator. Set it once in the master file to the version the paper used for the archive check, and to the current version for the rewrite.

**Python**

- `pandas` guesses column types on read, which turns "0.80" into 0.8 and can turn an identifier like "007" into 7. Read anything printed as text.
- `groupby` drops groups whose key is missing unless told otherwise (`dropna=False`), and sorts groups by default.
- `statsmodels`' array interface (`sm.OLS(y, X)`) does not add an intercept, while its formula interface does.
- Library defaults change between versions more often than in R or Stata. Pin every version, and expect dispatch drift of the kind described in [`traps.md`](traps.md).


<!-- file: agent/README.md -->

# Agent instructions

These files restate the guide as instructions a coding agent can follow. They add nothing to it. If one of them disagrees with the stage, rule, or schema it points to, the document written for people is correct, and the agent file should be fixed.

- [`session_start.md`](session_start.md): a prompt to begin each working session.
- [`00_setup.md`](00_setup.md) to [`06_publish.md`](06_publish.md): one file per stage.

They are written for no particular model or tool. To use them, point the agent at `session_start.md` and at the file for the stage you are working on, and keep the guide's `rules/`, `schemas/`, and `traps.md` where the agent can read them.

Two points apply to every stage. The author decides what counts as an error, whether a correction changes a conclusion, and what goes to a journal; the agent proposes. Every number the agent reports about the paper (a count, a coverage fraction, a verdict) must come from code it ran, not from memory of an earlier run.


<!-- file: agent/session_start.md -->

# Session start

Paste or point the agent to the following at the start of each working session, with the bracketed parts filled in.

---

You are helping me actively maintain the replication archive for one of my published papers: [citation], with its deposit at [deposit DOI], in the repository at [path].

Read these first:

1. The guide's README, and the stage file for the stage we are working on today: [stage], in both `stages/` and `agent/`.
2. `rules/erratum.md`, `rules/rounding.md`, `rules/stochastic.md`, `rules/severity.md`, and `traps.md`.
3. The schema in `schemas/` for every table you will write or read today.
4. The repository's `STYLE.md`, if it exists, and its notes from earlier sessions, if any.

Then tell me, in a few lines, the state of the repository: which stages are done according to each stage's "Done when" list, what is failing, and what you propose to do in this session. Wait for my answer before changing anything.

Ground rules for every session:

- Do not change, move, or delete anything in the downloaded deposit. Run deposited code only in a scratch copy.
- Never type a computed value into a table. Only the values printed in the article are transcribed; everything else is generated by code in the repository.
- Never use a published number as an input to the rewrite.
- When a check fails, find out why before changing the check.
- When you find a possible error in the paper, record the evidence and propose a classification. Whether it is an error, whether it changes a conclusion, and what to do about it are my decisions.
- Report every number about the paper from a command you ran in this session.
- Before ending the session, write down what you did, what is still failing, and what comes next, in the repository's notes.


<!-- file: agent/00_setup.md -->

# Stage 0 for agents: setup and style

Source of truth: [`stages/00_setup.md`](../stages/00_setup.md).

## Goal

A repository skeleton, the published record in hand, the deposit identified, and an approved `STYLE.md`.

## Do

1. Collect the publisher's rendered PDFs: the article (version of record), the online appendix, and any published corrigendum. Do not use a preprint or accepted manuscript as a source of published values.
2. Find the replication deposit and record its DOI. Do not copy the data into the repository.
3. Ask the author which materials outside the deposit exist (production `.tex` or `.docx`, proofs, accepted manuscript, old working scripts) and where they are. Treat a working-folder `.tex` as the published text only if its compiled PDF matches the publisher's.
4. Create the repository with the layout in the stage file: `run_all.R` (or the language's equivalent), `download_original.R`, `maintained/`, `maintained/output/`, `ground_truth/`, `errata.qmd`, `README.qmd`, a `.gitignore` that excludes `original/`, and a license.
5. Use paths relative to the repository root everywhere.
6. Read the recent code the author points you to, and draft `STYLE.md`: script organization, naming, data manipulation idioms, modeling defaults, figures (with a CSV of plotted values beside each), tables, and things to avoid. Quote examples from the author's code.
7. Give the draft to the author and revise it until they approve it. Commit the approved version.

## Do not

- Let `STYLE.md` override the paper's own choices. The rewrite keeps the original estimator, specification, sample, standard errors, and seed whatever `STYLE.md` prefers. Say so in `STYLE.md`.
- Use materials outside the deposit as inputs to the rewrite. They explain errors; they do not supply numbers.

## Stop and ask the author

- When you cannot find the deposit, or find more than one version of it.
- When a corrigendum or erratum exists and you are unsure which version of a passage is the one to check.

## Done when

The repository exists with its entry point and layout, the published PDFs are in hand, the deposit DOI is recorded, and an approved `STYLE.md` is committed.


<!-- file: agent/01_archive_check.md -->

# Stage 1 for agents: archive check

Source of truth: [`stages/01_archive_check.md`](../stages/01_archive_check.md). Schemas: [`original_manifest.md`](../schemas/original_manifest.md), [`archive_run_status.md`](../schemas/archive_run_status.md), [`archive_overwrites.md`](../schemas/archive_overwrites.md).

## Goal

A verified manifest of the deposit, a download script that stops on any discrepancy, and a record of what happens when the deposited code runs.

## Do

1. Build `original_manifest.csv` from the archive's API, not by hand, with every checksum the archive publishes and every file's byte size. For Dataverse, request each file in its original format.
2. Write `download_original.R` to download every listed file into `original/`, stop on any size or served-checksum mismatch, print any published-checksum mismatch, stop on any file in `original/` the manifest does not list (hidden files included), and unpack any zip or RAR into its own folder checked against a second manifest.
3. Make it the first step of `run_all.R`, and run it.
4. Before running any deposited code, search it for every call that writes a file, after joining continued lines.
5. Copy the deposit to a scratch folder and run each deposited script there, twice: once as shipped, and once with every intermediate file the deposit ships removed. Run under the software of the paper's day where it matters (for R code from before April 2019 that draws with `sample()`, `RNGkind(sample.kind = "Rounding")`). Capture printed output: in R, source with `print.eval = TRUE`.
6. Write one row per script per pass to `ground_truth/archive_run_status.csv`, including `not_run` rows with the reason for anything you could not run.
7. After each pass, compare every file with the manifest and write what was added, overwritten, rebuilt, withheld, or deleted to `ground_truth/archive_overwrites.csv`.

## Do not

- Run deposited code in `original/`, or edit any deposited file.
- Fix the deposited code. Record why each failure happened; the failures are part of the record.
- Treat a clean exit as reproduction. Whether the archive reproduces the paper is decided in Stage 2.
- Accept a deprecation warning, or a recorded "package removed", as the cause of a failure without testing it.

## Stop and ask the author

- When the published and served checksums disagree for a file that is not a converted tabular file.
- When a script needs software you cannot run (Stata, a licensed dataset).

## Done when

The manifest verifies, the download script stops on any mismatch, and every deposited script has a row in `archive_run_status.csv` for each pass.


<!-- file: agent/02_ground_truth.md -->

# Stage 2 for agents: ground truth

Source of truth: [`stages/02_ground_truth.md`](../stages/02_ground_truth.md). Schemas: [`ground_truth.md`](../schemas/ground_truth.md), [`float_coverage.md`](../schemas/float_coverage.md). Rules: [`rounding.md`](../rules/rounding.md), [`stochastic.md`](../rules/stochastic.md).

## Goal

One generated table comparing every printed number with the archive's value and the rewrite's value, and a coverage table saying how much of each float it checks.

## Do

1. List every table and figure from the article and appendix themselves, and write a row for each in `float_coverage.csv`.
2. Transcribe every printed value from images of the published pages, as strings, with their printed precision. Read multi-column tables from the rendered page, not from extracted text. Read numbers printed on a figure by position.
3. Write `ground_truth/build_ground_truth.R`, run last by `run_all.R`. It starts from the transcribed values and joins them to the archive's values (from the Stage 1 runs) and the rewrite's values (from `maintained/output/`, at full precision).
4. Compare at the printed precision, by formatting the computed value and comparing strings, after the normalizations in `rules/rounding.md`. Compare the archive at the coarser of the page's precision and the precision the deposited code printed.
5. For values from random draws, first confirm that something draws at random. For unseeded values, compare against the distribution over many seeds, leave `match_rewrite` as `NA`, and record the verdict in `holds`.
6. On every row where a comparison fails, set `defect_locus` where the row is built, and propose a `disposition`. Compute `corrected_here` from `errata_entries.csv`.
7. Make the build stop if: a printed value has been read as a number; a failing row has no locus or a passing row has one (apart from the documented exception); a `paper_internal` row has no disposition; any join is not one-to-one; or a float is missing from `float_coverage.csv`.
8. Compute every count in `float_coverage.csv`.

## Do not

- Type any value except the printed ones.
- Select a row by its printed value.
- Read the printed values with automatic type guessing.
- Count a float as covered because it has one row, or because it prints no numbers.
- Set a default locus for the whole table.

## Stop and ask the author

- When the page, the archive, and the rewrite disagree and you cannot tell which is wrong (propose `unresolved`).
- When a value is wrong in a way that may change a conclusion.

## Done when

The build runs last in `run_all.R` and passes all of its checks.


<!-- file: agent/03_rewrite.md -->

# Stage 3 for agents: maintained rewrite

Source of truth: [`stages/03_rewrite.md`](../stages/03_rewrite.md). Rules: [`erratum.md`](../rules/erratum.md). Style: the repository's `STYLE.md`.

## Goal

New code, on current packages, that reproduces every table, figure, and number in the paper from the deposited data.

## Do

1. Write one script per table or figure, named for what it produces, with cleaning separate from analysis and shared functions in one helpers file. Follow `STYLE.md`.
2. Write everything to `maintained/output/`. Beside every figure, write a CSV of every quantity it plots. Beside every formatted table, write its values unrounded.
3. Keep the paper's estimator, specification, sample, standard errors, and seed.
4. Correct unambiguous coding errors (a wrong variable, index, or column; a covariate the paper's description says should or should not be there; a rank-deficient model that silently dropped a column). Record each correction for the ground truth and the errata.
5. Use the current random-number generator. Where it moves a published number, the ground truth records `environment`.
6. Compare every rendered figure with the published one by eye, in addition to its numbers.
7. Blank the timestamps in PDF output.
8. Run `run_all.R` twice from fresh sessions, check both exit statuses, and confirm the second run leaves `maintained/output/` byte-identical.

## Do not

- Use any published number as an input. If a script seems to need one, the computation upstream is missing.
- Write a script that returns early because its output already exists.
- Accept a comment saying a number "can't be computed" from the deposit without trying.
- Change an analysis choice because `STYLE.md` or current practice prefers another.
- Carry a deposited bug into the rewrite because the archive has it.

## Stop and ask the author

- When it is unclear whether a discrepancy is a coding error or an analysis choice.
- When two deposited values are both defensible and the paper does not say which was meant.

## Done when

`run_all.R` runs from a clean session, every table and figure has a script that produces it, no published value is an input, and two runs in a row leave `maintained/output/` unchanged.


<!-- file: agent/04_claims.md -->

# Stage 4 for agents: claims

Source of truth: [`stages/04_claims.md`](../stages/04_claims.md). Schema: [`published_claims.md`](../schemas/published_claims.md). Verdict logic: [`languages.md`](../languages.md#the-claims-check).

## Goal

Every claim in the article and appendix, numeric or not, extracted, classified, and checked by code that quotes the sentence and recomputes it.

## Do

1. Extract every numeric token from the article and appendix, then sweep again for numbers written as words.
2. Read for claims with no number: significance, direction, order, persistence, and counts in words.
3. Classify each claim (`pipeline`, `descriptive`, `definitional`, `structural`, `transcribed`), store the printed value as text with its precision, and set `comparison` and `needs_block`. Write `ground_truth/published_claims.csv`.
4. Compare the `descriptive` and `definitional` classifications within each section, and make the same sentence construction get the same type.
5. Write `maintained/in_text_claims.R` with one block per claim with `needs_block = TRUE`. Each block quotes the sentence verbatim in a comment and recomputes the claim from `maintained/output/` or the cleaned data.
6. Where a block declares `range`, `derived`, or `shape`, make the block's code test the condition. For a hedged number, make the block test the half-step bound in `rules/rounding.md`, since the check does not.
7. Run the file on its own, and check that the printed claim ids are exactly the `needs_block` ids.
8. Reconcile with the ground truth: every claim in both must have the same printed value, precision, and type, and where both compute a value, they must agree.

## Do not

- Read the ground truth from the claims script. The two checks must be independent.
- Refit models in the claims script.
- Declare a verdict a block has not tested.
- Treat an unhedged approximation as hedged.
- Invent a computation for a quantity nothing in the paper or deposit identifies.

## Stop and ask the author

- When a claim with no number appears not to hold.
- When the two instruments disagree and you cannot tell which is wrong.

## Done when

Every claim is in `published_claims.csv`, every claim that needs a check has one, the printed count equals the declared count, the two instruments agree, and the summary line shows no failing verdicts.


<!-- file: agent/05_errata.md -->

# Stage 5 for agents: errata

Source of truth: [`stages/05_errata.md`](../stages/05_errata.md). Schema: [`errata_entries.md`](../schemas/errata_entries.md). Rules: [`erratum.md`](../rules/erratum.md), [`severity.md`](../rules/severity.md).

## Goal

One itemized errata note per paper, rendered to PDF, with every corrected value computed at render time, and a matching `errata_entries.csv`.

## Do

1. Draft an entry for every error the earlier stages found, and for errors found by reading the article against itself, its appendix, its code, its references (checked against Crossref), and any earlier correction.
2. For each entry, set `class`, `source`, and `form`; quote the published passage and write the corrected one, marking each changed span `[[like this]]`; write a note explaining what was wrong and what the correction rests on; and list the `claim_ids` it corrects.
3. Compute every corrected value from the rewrite's output when `errata.qmd` renders.
4. Make the render check that: every claim id exists; only `quantity` entries carry corrected values, one per id; every corrected value appears in the corrected passage; no corrected value renders identically to the published one at the printed precision; and no entry corrects a claim the pipeline reproduces.
5. Check every quotation against an image of the published page.
6. Order the entries by severity, most serious first, and propose which entries, if any, change a conclusion and which meet the bar for a corrigendum.

## Do not

- Include differences within simulation noise, findings you could not judge, or analysis choices.
- Type a corrected value.
- Quote from extracted PDF text without checking the page image.
- Renumber entries once the note is public. Add new entries at the end.
- Decide whether a conclusion changes, or whether anything goes to a journal.

## Stop and ask the author

- Before finalizing the list of entries: the author decides which candidates are errors.
- For every entry that might change a conclusion.
- Before anything is sent to a journal or to coauthors.

## Done when

`errata.qmd` renders without error, every corrected value is computed, every quotation has been checked against the published page, the render's checks pass, and every `paper_internal` row in the ground truth has a disposition.


<!-- file: agent/06_publish.md -->

# Stage 6 for agents: report and publish

Source of truth: [`stages/06_publish.md`](../stages/06_publish.md).

## Goal

A README a stranger can follow, a public repository with a permanent DOI, a link from the original deposit, and a scheduled check.

## Do

1. Write `README.qmd` for someone arriving from the article: what the repository is, a table of verified DOIs (article, deposit, repository), how to run it, an overview of the paper, whether the archive runs, the errata, the ground truth and each float's coverage, the two claim checks, the rewrite, and the software environment.
2. Compute every quantity in the README's prose with inline code.
3. Run the whole pipeline once more and confirm it leaves no stray or changed files. Check file names against a case-sensitive file system.
4. Write `.zenodo.json` with the title, creators, license, and related identifiers: the article (`isSupplementTo`), the deposit (`isDerivedFrom`), and the repository URL, listed explicitly.
5. Prepare the line that links the deposit to the maintained version (the Zenodo concept DOI and the repository URL), for Dataverse's Related Material field or the OSF project description.
6. Add the scheduled check workflow, and confirm it passes once.

## Do not

- Write the history of the project into the README.
- Copy the deposit into the repository.
- Pin old package versions to make a failing check pass; update the rewrite instead.

## Stop and ask the author

- Before making the repository public, creating a GitHub release, or publishing at Zenodo. Each is visible to others and hard to undo.
- Before editing any deposit's metadata. Deposits in a journal's collection, or made by a coauthor, need their curators or owners.

## Done when

The README renders with every number computed, the repository is public, its Zenodo DOI resolves and appears in the README and the errata, the original deposit links to it, and the scheduled check has passed at least once.
